items.title: October 2026 Jobs Report: Employment growth tops market forecasts
items.description: October 2026 Jobs Report: Employment growth tops market forecasts Written by Kenny Lee on November 6, 2026 Key findings U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while gains in September and August were revised up by a combined 84,000. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1% from 4.2% as strong employment growth absorbed an increase in labor force participation. Wage growth continued to cool compared to recent years, with average hourly earnings rising 3.1% year over year. What happened: The nonfarm payroll employment rose 165,000 in October, topping financial market expectations. Combined with strong upward revisions to increases in September and August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics report this month indicates a meaningful improvement in job growth. The increases in employment were broad-based across key industries such as professional and business services (+70,000); healthcare and social assistance (+55,000); and transportation and warehousing (+25,000). Employment in temporary help services, a leading indicator for overall labor demand, soared to 18,600. The household survey also indicates a resilient labor market. The labor force participation rate increased to 61.9% from 61.8% as more workers rejoined the workforce. Combined with strong increases in employment, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%. Why it matters for housing: Stable employment and wage growth give households the confidence to buy a home or sign a new lease, but the housing market is already feeling the chilling effects of the recent surge in mortgage rates. Zillow data points to a colder-than-usual fall market: our preliminary measure of existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year in October. Newly pending listings — a leading indicator of next month’s closed sales — fell 16.8% year over year, the biggest decrease since August 2023. With mortgage rates above 7%, affordability headwinds in the housing market may still feel insurmountable — even for those who have a job or recently found one. This is consistent with our expectation for a more substantial decline in existing home sales and slower growth in home value in Q4. While mortgage rates have been declining from their recent peak, it is difficult to know how far they will fall when forces pushing up Treasury yields, such as anxiety over government deficits and geopolitical impact on energy prices, remain at play. But when mortgage rates come down, eventually, buyers will be ready. The Bureau of Labor Statistics report today is consistent with a stable labor market in a growing economy. The resilient labor market will pave the way for a housing market thaw. items.title: October Jobs Report: Surging Payrolls and Hiring Uptick Means Fed Hawks Can Exhale
items.description: October Jobs Report: Surging Payrolls and Hiring Uptick Means Fed Hawks Can Exhale By Jake Krimmel Nov 06, 2026 October Payrolls Jump 165,000, More Than Double Expectations, With 84,000 Jobs Revised Up Today’s October jobs report was impressive. Coming in, we would have been happy with the forecasted 65,000, more than double last month’s. Instead we got more than double those expectations, with payrolls up 165,000. Revisions added another 84,000 jobs to August and September, lifting the three-month average to 137,000 from about 51,000 a month ago. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1%, just as the Chicago Fed predicted , while labor force participation rose to 61.9%, above the 61.8% expected. Both moved just a smidge, but together they are notable. Wages firmed too, up 0.4% in the month and 3.1% from a year ago, versus 3.0% in September. This is still a low hire, low fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side. The numbers could still be revised, of course, and the trend matters more than any one point; but you don’t get a good trend without a good month. A Strong Report Clears the Way for the Fed’s Next Hike For the Fed, this clears the way for a hike. After last month’s hot inflation print put the next increase in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory, a soft jobs report was the one thing that could have complicated December. If Fed hawks were waiting to exhale, they can do so now. CME FedWatch saw Fed hike odds increase, as anticipated. The 10-year yield edged up on the announcement, and yields and hike odds remain the two things to watch for mortgage rates. Midterms or Not, Housing Needs Real Wage Gains and Cooler Inflation One question that keeps coming up is whether the midterms changed anything for the housing market. In the short run, not much – the Iran War and its impact on inflation and mortgage rates remain the major wildcard. Getting back to “normal” in many metros takes more activity, which depends on improved buying power to bring buyers off the sidelines. Mortgage rates have declined for three straight weeks, to 7.18% , after a massive 74 basis point surge from late August to mid-October, but wages are the other half of buying power. That 3.1% annual wage growth is nominal, and it trails September’s 3.7% inflation and likely won’t keep up with where inflation is headed. Nominal wage growth is necessary but not sufficient for real wage gains in this environment, so inflation has to come back down too. A more dynamic labor market and cooling inflation are sorely needed for demand.

Economy In third quarter 2026, the Reno area recorded 287,200 jobs, with unemployment declining 20 basis points (bps) year-over-year (YOY) to 4.0%. The region continued to exhibit steady growth, with households increasing 1.7% YOY to 239,300. Wage growth remained a key driver of labor force expansion, as median household income reached $95,300, up 3.9% YOY. Supply & Demand The Reno multifamily market continued to tighten in third quarter 2026, with overall vacancy declining 230 bps YOY and 10 bps quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 5.5%, the lowest level since 2022. Improved occupancy was driven by continued tenant demand, as the market recorded 166 units of net absorption during the quarter and 898 units year-to-date (YTD), extending Reno's streak of positive net absorption to 17 consecutive quarters. The University submarket led both quarterly and YTD net absorption with gains of 61 units and 222 units, respectively, while South Reno added 31 units during the quarter and 176 units YTD. In contrast, Carson City County was the only submarket to post negative net absorption in the third quarter, recording a loss of eight units. Limited new supply further supported market fundamentals, with just 96 units completed during both the quarter and YTD, well below the 10-year average of 1,344 annual construction completions. Construction activity remains modest with only 698 units underway, including Village at Cross Creek in Carson City County and Argent Flats in South Reno. Tight conditions in several submarkets continued to constrain available inventory, particularly in areas near major employment centers and newer housing stock. As demand continues to outpace construction completions and the development pipeline remains limited, the market is well positioned for continued occupancy gains through the remainder of 2026. Pricing Average monthly asking rents increased 5.9% YOY to $1,813 per unit, while effective rents rose 7.1% YOY to $1,776 per unit. Rent growth remained broad-based across the market, with South Reno and Sparks/Spanish Springs posting the highest effective annual rent growth at 9.3%, followed by West Reno at 7.2% and the University submarket at 7.1%. South Reno continued to command the region's highest effective rent at $2,045 per unit, reflecting strong demand for newer product and amenity-rich communities. As vacancy continues to decline and development activity remains limited, rental rates are expected to maintain positive momentum through 2027. items.title: Mortgage rates fell and demand steadied as inventory dipped
items.description: Mortgage rates fell, demand stabilized and inventory had a noticeable decline last week. But are the changes in demand and inventory data about seasonality, or has the housing market changed with the recent mortgage rate decline? Let’s take a look at the weekend tracker and see what the data is telling us with rates falling the last three weeks. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% What a crazy time in the bond market recently: the key level of 5.35% has not only held since early October, but the reversal has been truly nice to watch. The midterm elections , which changed the control of the House and Senate, have added another variable into the mortgage rate equation. I discussed what Congress can do to help lower mortgage rates on this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler, but for now the head-and-shoulders pattern of the 10-year yield is still somewhat intact, though a fight for it to break lower is happening. I wouldn’t get too excited about mortgage rates until the 10-year yield can break under 4.70% and have follow-through bond buying, but mortgage rates have fallen and demand has stabilized over the last few weeks. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multiyear lows. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% — spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility. That said, if mortgage spreads weren’t near multiyear lows right now, we'd have no chance of getting mortgage rates below 7.25%, and demand wouldn't have stabilized recently. Now that spreads have moved up from this year's lows, we can clearly see that mortgage rates would be sub-7% if spreads return to that level. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.27% from 2.23% a week earlier. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle. If we had the best levels of spreads in 2026, mortgage rates would be 6.72% today, not 7.17% . If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.11% today, not 7.17% . Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. The key for the last three weeks: lower rates, even above 7%, have stabilized demand, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, this isn’t growth, just stabilization from a noticeable slowdown when mortgage rates got toward 7.60%. The last three years and 10 months show that housing demand grows when mortgage rates fall below 6.64% and head toward 6%; above 7%, we don’t have much growth data beyond seasonal demand. Last year at this time, mortgage rates were headed toward 6%, so the year-over-year comps will be hard for some time. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 51,764 2025: 59,164 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We had a small decline week to week; I can see the stabilization here as well and the year-over-year comps will also be very difficult here, as last year at this time rates were heading toward 6%. Earlier in the year, when rates were lower, pretty much every week this year showed growth. Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026: 16 positive week-to-week prints 24 negative week-to-week prints 5 flat week-to-week prints 10 weeks of double-digit year-over-year growth 25 weeks of positive year-over-year growth 15 negative year-over-year prints Housing inventory Housing inventory growth has been very tame this year, with some weeks being down year over year. However, when mortgage rates got above 6.64% and then headed toward 7.60%, we did see some growth pick up. Also, rates were lower last year so demand was heading toward a nine-month high in December, which means it the comps will be easier to show growth in inventory. Inventory growth is running at 7.18% even with easier comps. Weekly inventory change (Oct. 30-Nov. 6): Inventory fell from 914,833 to 902,740 Same week last year (Oct. 31-Nov 7): Inventory fell from 856,751 to 842,257 New listings New listings are in their typical seasonal decline; 2026 has been the healthiest new-listings year since 2022, with over 80,000 new listings per week a few times this year. The concern I had was that if higher rates cause sellers to stop listing their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 — that would hurt supply and demand. However, that hasn’t happened in any meaningful way. Most home sellers are buyers, and now that rates have fallen a smidge, it looks like we can end the year on a positive note for 2026 for new listings. In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years . Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years: 2026: 54,479 2025: 55,486 Price-cut percentage Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%; demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%. items.title: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October
items.description: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October by Kim O'Brien Posted November 6, 2026 in Market Research October marked the first month of rent cuts in the U.S. apartment market in 2026, but annual gains continue at a robust pace. Same-store effective asking rents increased 1.7% year-over-year, according to October data from RealPage Market Analytics . That was the market’s biggest annual price increase since May 2023. While the annual reading has improved, the gain stemmed less from robust monthly pricing and more from weak rent performance falling out of the annual calculation. In fact, rents came down a mild 0.7% during October, marking the first monthly rent cut in the U.S. in calendar 2026. U.S. apartment occupancy faded to 95% in October, easing 20 basis points (bps) from the September showing. Still, October occupancy is up 40 bps in the calendar year and remains 10 bps ahead of the October 2025 showing. Helping support occupancy and rent performance, the U.S. apartment market has seen supply and demand edge closer to balance recently. Renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, gaining ground on a cooling supply wave. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units in the past year, nearly half the recent peak from late 2024. Bay Area and Midwest markets still lead for rent growth Rent performance remained sharply split by market. Coastal tech hubs and Midwest metros delivered the strongest annual gains, while most Sun Belt markets kept logging rent declines. Northern California's tech-driven markets posted the three strongest gains among the 50 largest apartment markets in the year-ending October. San Francisco saw rents hike 14.7% over the past year, San Jose followed at 9.5%, and Oakland reached 8.5%. All three markets are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest markets make up much of the rest of the top 10 list. Milwaukee led the major Midwest markets with annual rent growth of 4.2%, followed by Chicago (3.3%), Kansas City (3.1%) and Cleveland (3.1%). Detroit and St. Louis both fell just shy of making the cut, with annual rent growth of 2.7% in each market. Sun Belt rents still trail, but the gap is narrowing The South region overall has returned to annual rent growth, though barely, at 0.5% in October. Sun Belt and Florida markets continue to see the nation’s steepest declines. San Antonio had the deepest cut among big markets at 2.6%, stemming from occupancy at 92.5%, also dead last among the largest 50 markets. Also posting rent declines in the year-ending October were Houston (-1.8%), Tampa (-1%), Charlotte (-0.9%) and Denver (-0.8%). The bigger story, however, is how many Sun Belt markets have stopped seeing rent positioning hemorrhage. Annual increases have returned to Phoenix (0.4%) and Austin (0.6%), as well as Atlanta (0.8%), Raleigh (1.0%), Miami (0.6%) and Jacksonville (2.6%). items.title: Camden lowers guidance after September concession resurgence
items.description: Camden lowers guidance after September concession resurgence The REIT still saw improvement in expenses and new lease growth in Q3, though rising interest rates forced it to cancel property and land acquisitions. Published Nov. 6, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Wall Street sign with american flags and New York Stock Exchange in Manhattan, New York City, USA. Getty Images Camden’s Property Trust lowered its 2026 same-store revenue midpoint by 50 basis points to 0% after a weaker-than-expected September and the expectation of greater seasonal decline in the fourth quarter, according to the REIT’s executives on Friday’s third-quarter earnings call. Performance in September, specifically, surprised the company and set the stage for that revision, according to CEO Alex Jessett. “It was a greater decline in traffic than we had expected,” Jessett said. “And when we had the decline in traffic, obviously, you have to reduce your prices if you're trying to increase traffic.” Jessett said concessions, which were “incredibly sticky,” ranged from three weeks in West Palm Beach, Florida, up to two months in Austin, Texas, as merchant builders continued to offer steep discounts. “The third quarter, at least July and August, were so strong that we would have expected to see others start to dial back their concessions, and they absolutely did not do it,” Jessett said. Despite the September slowdown, there were positives: Camden expects same-store YOY expense growth of 1.75%, which is 75 bps better than the REIT’s prior midpoint and 125 bps better than beginning-of-year guidance, according to CFO Ben Fraker. The company was also “the only S&P 500 multifamily REIT to experience sequential improvement for both new lease rates and blended lease rates each quarter this year, and we were the only one with second- to third-quarter acceleration,” according to Jessett. Camden saw positive signs into Q4, though high-concession markets weighed on results. The REIT finalized its massive California sale and multiple acquisitions, though the interest rate environment forced it to cancel other deals. Rent trends Like many companies in supply heavy markets, Camden saw new leases remain in negative territory in Q3, falling to -2% YOY, according to its Q3 earnings release. In Q2, Camden’s new lease rate came in 130 bps lower at -3.3%. In Q3, renewals rose 3.6% YOY, giving the REIT a blended rate of 1%. In Q2, renewals increased 2.8% YOY and blends were -0.2%. “While renewal growth was in line with our expectations, new lease and blended lease growth were at the low end of our anticipated ranges, likely driven by the persistent concessions that remain in many of our core markets and sub-markets,” Camden Chief Operating Officer Laurie Baker said on the Q3 call. Camden sent out renewal offers to residents with December and January expirations at an average increase of 4.5%, according to Baker. That isn’t the only positive indicator. “We have seen signed new leases improve pretty dramatically in October as compared to September, and when we look at our October numbers and we compare them to October of last year, we're seeing really significant improvement,” Jessett said. Southeast Florida, at 1.6% YOY revenue growth; Atlanta, at 1.5%; Dallas, at 0.8%; and Houston, at 0.6%, were the top markets for Camden in Q3, according to a company Securities & Exchange Commission filing. Concessions have played a role in their performance, according to Baker. “We're seeing the strongest markets in Atlanta, Southeast Florida, Dallas and Houston,” Baker said. “And so, where those lower concessions are, we're obviously getting a little more pricing power, and we're having the ability to improve our occupancy.” On the other end of the spectrum were Denver, with a 5% YOY revenue decline; Nashville at -3.1%; Tampa, Florida, at -1.3%; and Orlando, Florida, at -0.7%, according to the SEC filing. “We still are continuing to see Denver and Nashville as those that have concessions that have been persistent,” Baker said. Buying and selling In July, Camden closed its sale of 11 properties with 3,620 apartment homes to a BlackRock-managed vehicle for $1.6 billion, recognizing a gain of $1 billion. The REIT used approximately $0.9 billion to retire balances outstanding under its unsecured revolving credit facility and commercial paper program, according to the Q3 earnings release. The REIT used $125 million to fund its August property and land acquisitions; $50 million to repurchase shares in August and early September; and $495 million toward the redemption of $500 million of senior notes due in November and to pay down borrowings in its commercial paper program. It had $55 million remaining in cash investment accounts for general corporate purposes, Fraker said on the call. In Q3, the REIT acquired Camden Brandon, a 296-unit property in Tampa; Camden LoSo, a 343-unit property in Charlotte, North Carolina; and Camden Gulch, a 300-unit property in Nashville, Tennessee, for a combined $305.2 million, according to the release. Camden acquired a land parcel in Tampa for approximately $18.3 million and sold 2.6 acres of land in Los Angeles for approximately $10.7 million, according to the release. Camden canceled the purchase of two properties and one land parcel in Q3 after interest rates rose , according to Jessett. “We went back looking for price adjustments, and clearly the sellers were not quite willing to capitulate to what we were looking for,” Jessett said. The REIT has also decided not to move forward with Nashville and Denver development projects at this time. items.description: Lenders turn to cuts, AI as strong jobs point to rate hikes By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published November 06, 2026, 1:38 p.m. EST | Updated November 06, 2026, 3:35 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Discover why nonbank mortgage payrolls hit a 2026 low despite rising retail productivity gains. Expert Quote: "For housing, stronger hiring cuts both ways." — Sam Williamson, Senior Economist, First American. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Nonbank mortgage payroll estimates dropped to a low for 2026 ahead of broader employment gains last month, pointing to a persistent need to manage origination staffing with retail productivity initiatives that have not yet reduced costs but at least contained them. The statistics, combined with October's strong jobs report signaling a likelihood rates won't immediately fall further , suggest the industry is reducing origination staffing but are able to do so gradually as artificial intelligence has helped boost the number of loans closers handle. More jobs mean more income and more reasons to move, while a stronger economy could prolong the wait for mortgage-rate relief," Sam Williamson, senior economist at First American, wrote in an emailed press statement. items.title: October Job Growth Beats Expectations, Keeping a December Fed Hike on the Table
items.description: October Job Growth Beats Expectations, Keeping a December Fed Hike on the Table Published on November 6th, 2026 by Chen Zhao Takeaway: A strong jobs report gives the Fed permission to hike again in December should they want to. This morning’s data shows that 165,000 jobs were created in October and 84,000 more jobs were created in August and September than previously reported. That brings the six-month moving average of job creation to 83,000 jobs per month after briefly dipping into negative territory last fall. The professional and business services sector saw outsized gains with 70,000 jobs created in October, the strongest month in four years. If this doesn’t get revised away in coming months, it would be a significant data point to counter AI-related labor market anxiety. The unemployment rate ticked down very slightly by 0.03 pp to 4.14%. It had gotten as high as 4.5% last November before gradually drifting down. At this point, despite all the wild month-to-month swings after the BLS updated their methodology, it’s pretty clear the labor market strengthened meaningfully as the year went on. In recent months, the Fed has not been making their policy decisions based on the jobs report because they’re more worried about the inflation side of their mandate than unemployment. Today’s data allows them to continue that stance. Regarding the December 9th meeting, a hike is already mostly priced in. There’s still next Tuesday’s inflation data and one more jobs report before the meeting, but given the recent commentary from officials, a hike seems pretty likely. items.title: Hiring Rebounds in October, but Residential Construction Employment Declines
items.description: Hiring Rebounds in October, but Residential Construction Employment Declines November 6, 2026 Jing Fu No Comments The U.S. labor market rebounded in October, with nonfarm payroll employment increasing by 165,000 jobs and the unemployment rate declining to 4.1%. However, the improvement in overall employment contrasts with continued weakness in residential construction, where employment fell by 16,400 jobs, the largest monthly decline since March 2021. Despite the October rebound, the labor market has recorded job losses in seven of the past 22 months. Wage growth continued to moderate, with average hourly earnings rising 3.1% year over year in October, down from an upwardly revised 3.2% in September. Average hourly earnings reached $38.00. The continued deceleration in wage growth suggests easing wage pressures. National Employment According to the Employment Situation Summary reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), total nonfarm payroll employment increased by 165,000 in October, following an upwardly revised gain of 60,000 in September. Revisions to prior months were broadly positive, reversing last month’s downward revisions. August’s job growth was revised up by 53,000, from the 133,000 reported last month to 186,000, while September’s gain was revised up by 31,000, from an initial estimate of 29,000 to 60,000. Combined, these revisions added 84,000 jobs to previously reported totals, compared with the 60,000 downward revision reported in the prior month. Job growth has strengthened in 2026. Through October, monthly payroll gains have averaged 86,000 on the current data vintage, up from the 68,000 monthly average reported through September. This improvement reflects October's solid employment gain and upward revisions to August and September. The current pace compares with an average of just 10,000 per month in 2025 and 122,000 per month in 2024. Over the past 12 months, total nonfarm employment has grown by 885,000, compared with a 496,000 gain reported a month ago. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% in October from 4.2% in September. Over the month, the number of employed persons rose by 463,000, while the number of unemployed persons decreased by 41,000. Combined, the civilian labor force expanded by 421,000 in October, extending the labor force growth that began in August. Meanwhile, the labor force participation rate—the proportion of the population either looking for a job or already holding a job—rose 0.1 percentage point to 61.9% in October, marking its fourth consecutive monthly increase. However, the rate remains well below its pre-pandemic level of 63.3% recorded at the start of 2020. Among prime working-age individuals (aged 25 to 54), the participation rate remained unchanged at 83.7%, matching its level a year earlier. Outside of construction, employment gains in October were led by health care (+42,000) and transportation and warehousing (+25,000). Financial activities (+7,000) and retail trade (+6,000) also posted gains. These increases were partially offset by declines in leisure and hospitality (-13,000) and wholesale trade (-9,100). Construction Employment Employment in the overall construction sector declined by 3,000 jobs in October, marking its first monthly decline since February, following an upwardly revised gain of 16,000 in September. Within the industry, residential construction employment fell by 16,400, the largest monthly decline since March 2021. In contrast, non-residential construction employment increased by approximately 13,300. Residential construction employment stood at 3.3 million in October, including 921,000 workers employed by builders and remodelers, down from 922,000 in September, and approximately 2.3 million residential specialty trade contractors. The six-month moving average of residential construction employment changes worsened to a loss of approximately 4,583 jobs per month in October, from a loss of roughly 3,283 in September. Over the last 12 months, residential construction has shed a net of 40,200 jobs, marking the twentieth consecutive month of year-over-year decline. This represents a widening decline from the 26,100 job loss reported a month earlier. Residential construction employment remains 1,270,900 positions above its post-Great Recession low, with that cushion narrowing from 1,287,300 in September. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate for construction workers declined to 4.1% in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 4.3% in September. It remained at a relatively low level. items.title: ULI Emerging Trends Report: DFW Three-Peats as Top Market to Watch in 2027, Houston Holds Serve
items.description: ULI Emerging Trends Report: DFW Three-Peats as Top Market to Watch in 2027, Houston Holds Serve by Taylor Williams November 6, 2026 November 6, 2026 4 LAS VEGAS — For the third consecutive year, Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) has secured the top spot as the U.S. market with the best overall real estate prospects. That’s according to the Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027 report, which is jointly produced every year by the Urban Land Institute (ULI) and accounting firm PwC. After finishing third and fifth in the 2025 and 2026 rankings, respectively, Houston has more or less maintained the status quo, claiming the No. 6 ranking in the 2027 report. Austin, meanwhile, continued to slip in the rankings, ostensibly due to the market’s ongoing struggles to catch up to recent building booms in the industrial and multifamily sectors. The state capital’s real estate prospects ranked 21st on this year’s list, marking the third consecutive year in which the market has failed to crack the Top 10. In explaining the top ranking, ULI and PwC immediately pointed to t he Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE) , which launched in downtown Dallas earlier this year and has been credited with fueling the growth of a major new vertical within the local economy: financial services. The report identified two nameless financial institutions — known within the real estate community to be Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley — that are developing new office campuses in Uptown Dallas in conjunction with the debut of TXSE. According to the report, combined, these projects could bring as many as 8,800 new jobs to Dallas over the next decade. In addition, the report noted that DFW is a top market for new development of data centers, though a statewide moratorium on permitting of those facilities and questions about the state’s ability to meet power requirements represent concerns to actualizing some of those projects. Oversupply in the metroplex’s industrial market is also burning off thanks to strong absorption of large-format facilities, while absorption of office space is also on the rise in conjunction with residential conversion projects that are putting dents in the existing inventory of vacant office space. Lastly, the report cited the decisions of both the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks and NHL’s Dallas Stars to pursue new arenas and surrounding mixed-use districts as fresh sources of growth on the retail, restaurant and entertainment sectors. items.title: NYC Claims Nearly Half Of State's Opportunity Zones, Putting New Neighborhoods In Play
items.description: The opportunity zone guessing game is over. On Thursday, the Treasury Department released the official list of census tracts eligible for the federal tax incentive program's second iteration, giving investors sitting in Park Avenue towers a new map to pore over. Pexels/Raphael Loquellano Brooklyn’s Bedford-Stuyvesant is among the neighborhoods designated as opportunity zones. “About $100B was deployed in the last decade to the program, probably half of that was quote-unquote institutional capital,” Ackman-Ziff Real Estate Group Director Andrew Rudy said. “I wouldn't be surprised if there was a doubling of capital formation for this iteration of the law versus the last.” Leading up to the release, New York was among the few states to publicize little information about the process. Stricter requirements for census tracts qualifying as “economically distressed” and Congress’ aim of funneling more money toward rural areas raised concerns over which New York City neighborhoods would be selected. The final deadline for states to submit their opportunity zone nominations was Oct. 28, after which Treasury reviewed them before releasing the full list. New York ultimately had 430 census tracts designated as opportunity zones, 210 of which are in the five boroughs. Brooklyn and the Bronx received the greatest number of designations, with 67 and 57, respectively. Another 41 are in Manhattan , 35 are in Queens and 10 are on Staten Island . The program allows investors to defer capital gains taxes and lower the basis on which they are taxed by investing in real estate projects or businesses that spur economic growth in select low-income communities. OZ 1.0, created under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 , used 2010 census data, allowing several neighborhoods already booming with development to qualify. It also gave benefits to projects in tracts adjacent to qualifying zones — a loophole that was removed from 2.0 — further drawing investment to highly developed neighborhoods. Because OZ 2.0 is based on the 2020 census, many areas that benefited the most under the program’s predecessor no longer qualify. Still, New York City’s density, alongside public housing developments and rent-stabilized units, means that some neighborhoods that don’t seem blighted qualify under the poverty threshold. The new map includes parts of Manhattan’s Lower East Side , Harlem and the Upper West Side , but the more appealing sites may be in areas where developers can layer subsidies, according to Ackman-Ziff Director Jordan Brustein. “For example, Yonkers , which is a more emerging area, is still well located on the transportation line and near the city. Developers are able to get unique incentives that yield better returns, which ultimately end up attracting more equity,” Brustein said. “So to us, we're more interested there than maybe even some of these better-located assets that have thinner return profiles.” Prized areas of the outer boroughs include Brooklyn’s Bedford-Stuyvesant , which has become increasingly gentrified, and areas of the East Bronx near the Metro-North’s station expansion. Queens’ Sunnyside Yards , where Mayor Zohran Mamdani is seeking to advance a 12,000-unit residential development , also received designation, despite not being on the initial list of eligible tracts. It is only one of two tracts nationwide to do so, with the other being in Hawaii. But unlike rural areas of the country, where the primary issue for development is attracting capital interest, New York City developers struggle with policies that make building more difficult. Under 485-x , higher construction wage requirements kick in for larger housing projects. As a result, the vast majority of proposals filed in the last two years are for buildings with 99 units or less. Rudy and Brustein said many investors are gravitating toward shovel-ready sites eligible under 1.0 as they raise capital for 2.0. Despite stronger markets like Long Island City no longer being included, the two-year transition period allows developers to continue accepting funds. Faced with higher interest rates and stricter lending standards , some developers in OZ 1.0 zones have pushed through the predevelopment process only to stall out before getting shovels in the ground. As long as they’ve followed compliance, those projects are likely to be among the first to be injected with OZ 2.0 funds. “Think about it this way: There’s a reason why they’re not in 2.0 maps,” Brustein said. “The capital markets have been challenging, and the one bright spot right now in the market is opportunity zones .” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Ackman-Ziff Real Estate Group , Brooklyn , Manhattan , Opportunity zones , opportunity zones 2.0 , Queens , Staten Island , Sunnyside Yards , The Bronx

items.title: Offices at Atlanta Financial Center slated for residential conversion
items.description: Offices at Atlanta Financial Center slated for residential conversion by John Yellig November 06, 2026 The three-building Atlanta Financial Center will be rebranded APEX Atlanta. Via Peachtree Commercial Real Estate. An office complex familiar to anyone who travels through Buckhead on GA-400 is set to be repositioned with over 200 apartments, improved office space and a new crown. The three-building Atlanta Financial Center, which straddles the busy highway, will be rebranded APEX Atlanta, according to Newmark , which is serving as exclusive leasing agent on behalf of the owner, Banyan Street Capital, which purchased the property in July 2025. The 284,000-square-foot office tower, APEX South, will be converted into a live/work building with approximately 260 residential units, while the 241,000 square-foot APEX North office tower on Peachtree Road has already undergone a $4 million capital improvement program that added a new lobby and on-site café to replace a former bank branch. The 386,000 square-foot APEX Tower is slated for a comprehensive redevelopment that will take the 19-story building down to its slabs and columns and rebuild it with a new curtain wall façade, lobby, elevators, town hall and conference center, rooftop skydeck and architectural crown. Additional details on APEX Tower and APEX South will be announced later. The overall goal is to reposition the entire property as a "premier Buckhead mixed-use destination." “The launch of APEX Atlanta reflects our conviction in Buckhead and establishing a new beginning for this irreplaceable landmark property,” said Zac Gruber, principal and president of the Office Division at Banyan Street Capital. “Tenant demand in Buckhead continues to concentrate in the highest-quality buildings, and we are approaching each of the three towers with a distinct strategy to meet it. items.title: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak
items.description: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak by Kim O'Brien Posted November 5, 2026 in Insights San Diego apartment supply hit a record high in the past year and is set to peak in 1st quarter 2027. In the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, roughly 6,600 units completed across San Diego, marking the highest annual total since Realpage Market Analytics began tracking the market in 2000. Supply in the past year also surpassed the market’s decade average around the 4,000-unit mark. Annual supply in San Diego is expected to remain elevated, peaking in the year-ending 1st quarter 2027, when roughly 6,880 units are scheduled for completion. After that, supply is slated to come down, aligning closer to the market’s decade average by the end of 2027. Demand is keeping pace with record apartment supply in San Diego, as evidenced by occupancy at 95.7% in October and rents up 1.5% year-over-year. After supply hits its peak and starts to come down, this market is projected to see improvement in both of those metrics. items.title: Progress Residential to pay $49.8M to settle FTC, state claims over rental practices
items.description: Progress Residential , the property manager of single-family rental homes owned by Pretium Partners , has agreed to pay $49.8 million to settle deceptive and unfair practices claims by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state regulators. The company denies any wrongdoing. In a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia , regulators alleged that the company advertised rental prices that did not reflect the full amount tenants would be required to pay, imposed hidden or inadequately disclosed fees and charges, and mishandled security deposits. The claims also included that Progress misrepresented the condition and move-in readiness of properties, restricted tenants’ ability to share reviews, and failed to adequately address tenant complaints and maintenance issues. In a statement given to HousingWire , a representative of Progress Residential and Pretium said the companies have reached an agreement “with the FTC and four states to resolve the Commission’s Civil Investigative Demand related to certain aspects of our resident experience during the period of 2021 to 2025.” “The agreement contains no admission of wrongdoing, and we maintain Progress’ practices have been transparent, fair, and consistent with industry practice,” the spokesperson said. “Although we disagree with the FTC’s claims, this resolution allows us to move forward with our mission of expanding access to quality, affordable rental housing in neighborhoods of opportunity.” The deal was reached by the FTC, the attorneys general of Arizona, Indiana and Colorado, and the Utah Division of Consumer Protection . It combines monetary relief for renters across the country. “We will always welcome investment in housing and recognize the important role private capital can play in increasing opportunities for Hoosier families,” Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said in a statement. “But no company, regardless of size or financial backing, gets a free pass to mislead consumers, impose hidden charges or treat tenants unfairly.” “Consumers searching for housing should have access to straightforward information about the costs associated with renting a home,” said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “Transparency regarding rental prices and fees helps consumers compare options and make informed choices. Clear pricing practices also support competition by allowing housing providers to compete on the basis of price, quality and service. "The FTC is monitoring the rental housing market and will continue to take action where appropriate to ensure that consumers receive clear and accurate information about the costs of renting a home.” Per the settlement terms, Progress must disclose the total monthly rental price in advertisements and listings, along with mandatory fees and charges, before a consumer commits to rent. The company also must stop withholding funds for ordinary wear and tear and is prohibited from misleading claims about property conditions. The consumer redress funds created by the settlement total $48.5 million and will be used for relief as directed by the stipulated order entered in the federal case. Arizona is receiving $1.25 million. In 2024, Invitation Homes , the largest owner of U.S. single-family rental homes, agreed to pay $48 million to consumers and change some of its practices. Editor's note: This story was updated with a statement from the FTC. Related More: Federal Trade Commission Pretium Partners Single-Family Rentals

items.title: U.S. job gains bounce back in October
items.description: U.S. job gains bounce back in October by Chuck Ehmann Posted November 6, 2026 in Insights The U.S. labor market came roaring back in October after September’s initial estimated gain of 29,000 new jobs with a reported increase of 165,000 jobs for the month, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Revisions to the August and September numbers boosted previous estimates by a combined 84,000 additional jobs, bringing the year-to-date total through October to 861,000 jobs gained compared to 116,000 total jobs added in all of 2025. Industry gains were led by Professional/Business Services (+70,000 jobs), Education/Health Services (+53,000 jobs), Trade/Transportation/Utilities (+22,000 jobs), and Manufacturing (+19,000 jobs). Particularly strong subsectors include temp services, management and consulting, social assistance, hospitals, couriers and messengers, warehouse clubs, and computer and electronic manufacturing. The remaining industries experienced modest gains or moderate shortfalls. Losses were especially deep in Leisure/Hospitality Services (-13,000 jobs) with much of that decline in food services and drinking places (-7,200 jobs). Meanwhile, the U3 seasonally adjusted headline unemployment rate (from the survey of households) decreased slightly to 4.1% in October, remaining in a narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March. This post is part of a series analyzing employment data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. For more on this data, read previous posts on Job Growth . items.title: Why didn’t the strong jobs report send mortgage rates skyrocketing?
items.description: With all the crazy things happening this week, the blowout jobs report on Friday didn’t send mortgage rates up at all. But one thing is for sure: the labor market has been better in 2026 than it was in 2025. I once labelled the labor market the honey badger labor market and no matter what has been thrown at the U.S. economy after 2011 — outside the brief recession created by COVID-19 — the labor data has held up well. Let’s dig into why very strong jobs report didn’t push yields or mortgage rates higher, as we would normally expect with the Fed being so hawkish in their statement. From BLS : Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. The labor data has improved enough that we have gone from a 4.5% unemployment rate last year to 4.1% today. Part of this is that labor-force growth has slowed and the break-even number has decreased, meaning fewer jobs are needed to keep the unemployment rate low. I have my break-even at 78,000 jobs created per month; I believe the Fed's is 33,000. Some economists have it at zero, which I think is silly. In any case, the unemployment rate is lower this year versus last year. Now, the low point in the COVID-19 recovery was about 3.4% unemployment back in 2023, so the unemployment rate has increased from that low, but it's still good enough to keep the Fed’s focus on inflation instead of labor. Jobs breakdown This month's report had growth in a few sectors, especially the business services sector jobs with one of the biggest monthly prints in years. There was also growth in manufacturing, and transportation & warehouse, while construction jobs faded a tad. Construction labor will be interesting in the future if mortgage rates stay elevated and short-term rates go up. If there is an AI slowdown and fewer AI data centers are being built, will this sector start to decline? One of my most critical recession indicators, residential construction employment, doesn’t look great lately, but it isn’t looking terrible either. In previous cycles, you can see a clear downtrend in this labor pool, which hasn’t happened in this cycle. With builders doing more rate buydowns — which have kept new home sales at 2019 levels over the past few years — and remodeling work holding up, this clear recession indicator hasn’t broken yet. 10-year yield and mortgage rates As crazy as this week has been, the jobs data wasn’t the big driver of mortgage rates as much as AI stock prices. CoreWeave's stock price was up 10% pre-market today, and bond yields ticked up with that. The jobs report didn’t do much to yields, we just saw a mild increase and then they fell back in line with the trend. Then CoreWeave stock price went almost negative, bond yields fell to the lows of the day, and now both have picked up from the lows! The market needs a weekend break. Mortgage rates ended the day flat at 7.17%, so as crazy as this sounds, the blowout jobs data didn’t send mortgage rates or bond yields much higher. That's good news for rates, and there are some levers the new Congress can pull to potentially get rates even lower, which I discussed on today's episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler. Conclusion A lot has changed this week for the economy regarding the bond market and where mortgage rates can go. The blue wave has raised hopes that the trade war and the conflict with Iran can end soon, AI companies have shown they can bleed, and Congress will try to slow the AI boom as much as it can without crashing it. All these things happened this week, so that even with four solid jobs reports during jobs week, the 10-year yield closed at 4.86% and mortgage rates closed at weekly lows. Related More: Jobs Report

items.title: Opendoor says it's behind schedule but plans to catch up by 2027
items.description: Opendoor is behind schedule. Since taking over the company a little over a year ago, CEO Kaz Nejatian has promised that the firm would achieve adjusted net income positive status on a 12-month go-forward basis by the end of 2026. But the recent housing market downturn, triggered by the rapid rise in mortgage rates , has proven to be a bit of a roadblock. “We are currently behind but we intend to catch up,” the iBuyer’s third quarter 2026 earnings report explained. During the quarter, Opendoor recorded an adjusted net loss of $66 million and an actual net loss of $218 million, up from a $90 million net loss a year ago. This comes even as the company reported a 12% annual increase in revenue to $1.022 billion. “A year ago, I told you we would build a different Opendoor — faster, stronger, fully committed to our mission of tilting the world in favor of homeowners,” Nejatian said during his firm’s earnings call with investors and analysts on Thursday. “We have spent the past year building a machine, and that machine is getting better every single day. We are not done yet. It is not perfect, but it is getting better every single day. The question is this: Is Opendoor in a better economic condition than it was a year ago? The answer is obviously yes.” A more resilient Opendoor Nejatian’s confidence comes from his belief that Opendoor has become more resilient over the past year. This includes ways in which the company has worked to serve more sellers without adding more homes to the company’s balance sheet. “This past week, around half of the first offers our direct-to-consumer sellers accepted were listing or Cash Now, More Later. That lets us serve more sellers with less of our capital exposed to changes in the market,” Nejatian said. In the past 12 months, the company has done over $1 billion in Cash Now, More Later volume. “We have built more ways to meet sellers' needs and have made it easier for them to understand their options and make the choice they want for their own lives,” Nejatian said. “Sellers can now adjust the offer slides and make the choice that is good for their families.” Scaling without buying more homes? Nejatian noted that every other time Opendoor has tried to scale, it has done so by purchasing more properties, but that isn’t the case this time. “We proved that we can grow without buying growth. That's the single most important thing that has happened over the last year. We're changing that with our capital-light products,” Nejatian said. Still, Opendoor did purchase far more homes in Q3 2026 than it did in Q3 2025, with a 316% year-over-year increase to 4,865 homes. The company’s signed acquisition volume represented an estimated 0.56% of market share in the addressable U.S. market in Q3 2026 — more than four times higher than a year ago. On the sales side, Opendoor sold 2,728 homes, an increase of 160 homes compared to a year ago. At the end of the quarter, the iBuyer had 7,596 homes in its inventory, up from 3,139 homes a year ago. While the increase in inventory could be seen as cause for concern, especially heading into the slower winter housing market, Opendoor noted that homes listed for sale for 120 days represented just 18% of inventory at the end of the quarter, down from 50% a year ago. Despite the progress, Nejatian said the company still has work left to do on unit economics and resale velocity, something it needs to focus on as it strives for more resiliency. “We're not as good as we want to be, but we're in a much better place," he said. "When the market moves against you and you own homes, there's two things you can do. You can sell fast, or you can hold and wait and pray for the market to recover. We choose to clear. "The decline in late August and September knocked us off track on execution a little bit because we turned our attention to clearance rather than margin improvement. It costs something real in a quarter like this, but that's the right way to run this company for the long run.” To help with some of these challenges, Nejatian said Opendoor has turned to AI to help improve speed while still scaling. Some of these tools include an AI model that determines repair plans for every home to hit the market. The company said the system has been outperforming the old process of following a standard repair manual. Opendoor said it also built a system to help price homes. While humans still have final judgment, the software does the work of pulling applicable, comparable homes. Ancillary services and the future Nejatian also said that Opendoor is focusing on its mortgage division . In Q3, Opendoor said originations from its in-house lender were up 400% year over year. This comes as the iBuyer's lender is now licensed in 25 states, compared to none a year ago. In addition, the company also launched a beta test of Buy with Opendoor in the San Francisco Bay Area this week. The product allows the company to earn mortgage revenue on properties not affiliated with Opendoor in anyway. Looking to the future, Nejatian said Opendoor is hoping to build out title and escrow services — not only to add more efficiencies to Opendoor’s in-house transactions but to add additional revenue streams by serving consumers not in its ecosystem. “We need to grow, use less capital per transaction, and sell homes faster. Those are things we can control, and that is what we are focused on. What matters to us is solving the core problems of our business, and those are what we need to focus on,” Nejatian said. items.title: Zillow's agent tie-ins grab purchase share as market shrinks
items.description: Zillow's agent tie-ins grab purchase share as market shrinks By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 05, 2026, 4:39 p.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 4:45 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Zillow's strategy of pairing its loan officers with invitation-only real estate agents is pulling purchase business away from the rest of the market. Its home loans unit grew purchase volume 55% in the third quarter while industry purchase originations fell. Processing Content Zillow Home Loans originated $1.972 billion of purchase loans in the third quarter, up from $1.276 billion a year earlier. Year-to-date volume is up 79%. Over the same quarter, Zillow estimates industry purchase origination volume declined 4%. "It's why purchase mortgage revenue for us is outgrowing the category even with the category declining," said CEO Jeremy Wacksman on the earnings call. The company is almost entirely a purchase lender. It did just $4 million of refinance production in the third quarter, versus $5 million one year prior. Second quarter volume was $2.181 billion, with only $7 million coming from refi. How the Preferred program feeds Zillow Home Loans The volume growth came as Zillow expanded the share of buyer connections sent through its Preferred program, an invitation-only network of real estate agents. Zillow previously called the program Flex. Executives reported double-digit adoption of Zillow Home Loans among customers working with Preferred agents. In Zillow's oldest markets, that rate is approximately 20%. "We are pleased that we continue to see double-digit customer adoption rates in Zillow Home Loans with our oldest markets at approximately 20% adoption rates, demonstrating that our integrated experience is adding value for both consumers and real estate agents," said Jeremy Hoffman, chief operating and chief financial officer. Wacksman framed the integrated model as the reason for Zillow's confidence in mortgage growth. "I mean 80% of buyers need both the mortgage and the agent. They want that as a one-stop shop," he said. "When we can offer that as an integrated experience, that's what they're choosing." He added that "a key part of this strategy is making sure that the Home Loans loan officer and the Preferred agent build a mutually beneficial relationship." The shift also changes how Zillow gets paid. Under its legacy advertising model, real estate agents used co-marketing dollars from lenders when bidding on leads, said Douglas Harter of BTIG. Under the Preferred model, Zillow captures mortgage revenue at origination, which can come six to 12 months later. Why mortgage revenue still missed The volume gains did not translate into the revenue analysts expected. Mortgage revenue rose 32% year-over-year to $70 million, but Keefe, Bruyette & Woods had forecast $81.3 million, putting the result 13.9% short. BTIG had forecast $81 million. Hoffman attributed the miss to " rate shock , which caused lower conversions." Industry purchase volume also came in weaker than Zillow planned for. "We estimate that industry mortgage purchase origination volumes were down 4% for Q3, below our expectation for a low-single-digit decline," he said. "We call out mortgage industry performance because the majority of Zillow buyers purchased their home with a mortgage." Harter tied the broader earnings miss to a weakening housing market and the "accelerated transition from the legacy ad model to Flex." Zillow underperformed existing home sales for the first time since the fourth quarter of 2024, which helped spread the miss into mortgage, he said in a research note. Zillow posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, compared with $10 million of net income in the third quarter of 2025. Zillow expects a steeper purchase decline in Q4 Zillow guided fourth quarter mortgage revenue to between $55 million and $56 million, with total revenue between $635 million and $665 million. "Our revenue outlook includes our expectation for a decline in year-over-year mortgage industry purchase origination volumes of 10% to 15%," Hoffman said. "This is down significantly from our prior industry expectation of mid-single-digits decline due to the sharp increase in mortgage rates we saw at the end of Q3 and into the start of Q4." Zillow expects 20% revenue growth in the fourth quarter as it scales outside its residential business, "with mortgage tailing off," Harter said. "The weakening housing market and bigger-than-anticipated model transition impact contributed to an 8-9% reduction in the 4Q revenue guide from the prior implied level," he said. "Headwinds are expected to carry into '27." Brad Finkelstein Originations Editor Brad Finkelstein is the originations editor of National Mortgage News. items.title: GSE delinquencies climb: Don't shift staff solely to FHA
items.description: GSE delinquencies climb: Don't shift staff solely to FHA By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 06, 2026, 4:11 p.m. EST | Updated November 06, 2026, 5:21 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: Whether mortgage servicers can maintain enough resources to handle rising agency loan distress Supporting Data: 6.9%: The late-summer increase in short-term delinquent GSE-backed mortgages. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. A late-summer rise in delinquencies among mortgages backed by the government-sponsored enterprises points to an upward trend that may require servicers to keep resources available for agency loans until economic conditions improve. Processing Content Delinquency totals increased on a month-to-month basis across stages in August, according to data provided by the Federal Housing Finance Agency, the overseer of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. The number of borrowers 30 to 59 days delinquent climbed 6.9% to 313,254 from 292,965 between July and August . The number of mortgages past due by 60 days or more grew 2.9% to 256,999 units compared to 249,816 one month earlier. The representative share of delinquencies relative to all outstanding GSE-backed mortgages now stands at 1.03% for early-stage distress. Liens 60 to 90 days past due make up 0.84% of outstanding mortgages. Borrowers in serious delinquency or currently in foreclosure account for 0.6%. Although mortgage leaders in 2026 raised regular warnings about looming challenges for borrowers with Federal Housing Administration mortgages , the new data hints at difficulties surfacing in the agency segment. While distress eased in the early summer, delinquency volumes finished August higher than where they stood at the end of the first quarter, when they settled at 281,098 and 246,081, respectively. FHFA's findings suggest rising prices and economic uncertainty continue to take a significant toll on the ability of some homeowners to consistently meet monthly mortgage obligations, with downward pressure on affordability becoming more acute as 2026 progresses. The surge in summer delinquencies came at the same time prices of consumer goods ticked upward, with energy costs, in particular, accelerating from the impact of the Iran War. Meanwhile, the still-rising costs of property insurance and taxes are leading to prolonged sticker shock, even as the pace appears to be leveling off this year. Recent forecasts predict many of the same factors will weigh on affordability through next year. The extent of homeowner concerns showed up in the number of calls for legal assistance to deal with potential foreclosures in the late summer, which came in almost 15% higher at the end of the third quarter compared to a year ago. Lawyers at LegalShield specifically noted inflation's effect on household budgets as a primary cause , rather than poor planning on the part of borrowers. Foreclosure starts leap 18% FHFA's new report also found foreclosures on the rise among Fannie Mae- and Freddie Mac-backed loans. The number of foreclosure starts shot up 18% to 8,930 from 7,569 from July to August. Foreclosure and bank sales of properties eased 5%, though, to 1,333 from 1,403. A report from Auction.com saw such inventory likely to increase for the remainder of 2026, but much of the growth will be driven by FHA foreclosures. The FHFA also recorded 7,675 permanent loan modifications in August, increasing from 7,503 a month earlier. More than one-third, or 36.5%, of modifications involved extending the term of payment. In total, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac completed 16,335 actions in August aimed at foreclosure prevention. items.description: Tucked into a private-club community in Hawaii called Kukui‘ula , two luxury homes just hit the market on Kauai's South Shore . Set right on the ocean, and set among lush tropical vegetation, this walkable community is only 25-minute drive from Lihue Airport. "The close proximity of everything is very convenient. You’re not having to spend a lot of time in the car,” says Pancho Sullivan of Hawaii Life , who is co-listing the two homes with Haunani Sullivan as well as Suzanne Harding and Jeff Skinner of Kukui‘ula Realty Group . The asking price sits at $9,900,000 each. Both were built in 2025 and have never been occupied. Aepo Nei 18 and Aepo Nei 19 are neighboring 3,372-square-foot homes with four bedrooms and 4.5 baths each. They can be purchased together, to create a private compound, or by separate buyers. Even better, the homes are fully furnished and stocked with items like bed and bath linens, beach towels, and everything you need to cook and serve in the kitchen, such as bowls, plates and glasses. Loading... Aepo Nei 18’s layout features connected pavilions. Steven Lippman / homesbystevenlippman.com Loading... The homes both feature 180-degree ocean views. Steven Lippman / homesbystevenlippman.com Loading... The homes feature lush living areas. Loading... The homes were constructed with natural materials like lava stone, coral and teak. Steven Lippman / homesbystevenlippman.com But it’s the design by Brazil-based Architects+CO that’s truly unique. Kauai Bahia Construction and their in-house material company, Kayu, handled all of the finish material production and millwork installation. "Brazil is known for incredible resort-club communities," says Pancho. "We actually traveled to Brazil to look at some of the clubs they designed. It’s the same tropical feel (as Hawaii) that blends in really well with nature." Aepo Nei 18’s layout features connected pavilions while Aepo Nei 19’s living spaces open onto a lawn courtyard. Design features at both include deep roof overhangs, walls of glass and multiple outdoor living spaces such as an infinity-edge pool; jacuzzi; swim-in, swim-out sauna; and in-water fire pit. "They both have beautiful 180-degree ocean views looking across the Tom Weiskopf -designed golf course. The swim-in, swim-out dry sauna facing the ocean is a unique feature," says Pancho, adding that the usage of natural materials like lava stone, coral and teak "fit into the landscape very beautifully." Referred to as the Garden Island, Kauai is home to about 73,000 people. "We get the majority of the island’s sunshine down here," says Haunani, about the South Shore. "People flock here for the beaches and the sunshine, Hawaiian monk seals on the sand, and a lot of ocean activity including surfing. "A lot of people that venture to Kauai are adventure seekers. We have great hiking. You can get on a boat and dive on the Nā Pali Coast and do ziplining and ATV tours." Loading... The exterior Aepo Nei 19’, which features deep roof overhangs. Stand-up paddleboarding, diving and fishing are two other activities easy to do in this community. Homeowners become club members with access to dining, a pool, spa (boasting a steam rook and lava-rock dry sauna), pickleball and tennis courts, and an 18-hole golf course. "There’s an incredible gym with classes daily, from yoga to sound bathing to fitness training," says Pancho. "All of that is part of your club membership. It’s a great place to be in tune with nature and get healthy." A 10-acre organic garden features a farm stand as well as opportunities to create floral bouquets. There’s also a conscious effort to honor Hawaiian history through cultural-heritage walks; sunrise ceremonies; hula performances; and classes in Hawaiian featherwork, quilting and basket weaving. “Members who are part of the club become life-long friends,” says Haunani. “They’re going to each other’s second homes and weddings. They travel around the world together.” The community also organizes annual golf and pickleball tournaments for members, and three golf courses are within a seven-minute drive. Loading... Like it's neighbor, the home features 180-degree ocean views. Loading... The living areas open onto an open courtyard and pool area. Another incentive is that the community’s zoned as a Vacation Destination Area. This means properties can join the short-term rental pool, for minimum seven-night stays. "Some of the owners put their homes in the rental pool and block out time for themselves and their families. That’s a great added benefit," says Haunani, as few club communities on Kauai allow this. The Sullivans think the buyer will likely hail from the West Coast, enticed by a direct flight from hubs in cities like Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix and Denver that arrive on the island by mid-day. “Kukui‘ula is a great place for families to gather and spend time together. We see a lot of members bring their entire families so they can vacation together multiple times per year,” says Pancho. “With all these activities it’s easy to curate an incredible vacation with the convenience of being on property. A lot of people enjoy coming here and decompressing.” Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now Based in Milwaukee, Kristine Hansen writes for TravelandLeisure.com, ArchitecturalDigest.com, Vogue.com, and other outlets. items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Real Estate Leader Shelton Wilder Reveals the Design Trends Set To Define Luxury Living in 2027
items.description: Real estate powerhouse Shelton Wilder has revealed that luxury homes in 2027 could be getting a warmer, more personal makeover—with an emphasis on spaces that feel as good to live in as they look. From richer wood finishes to rooms designed for relaxation, Wilder opens up about what she expects buyers to seek in homes while speaking exclusively to Realtor.com® . For homeowners preparing to sell, however, that doesn't necessarily mean taking on an expensive renovation to keep up. Instead, her predictions point to a preference for thoughtful design, practical amenities, and improvements that suit the property itself. Warmth and character take priority When it comes to the look of luxury homes in the coming year, Wilder anticipates a continued focus on natural finishes and enduring appeal. “We're going to see luxury homes continue moving toward warmth, character, and timeless design. Buyers want homes that feel beautiful but also comfortable and livable,” she says. “We're seeing more natural materials, beautiful wood tones, interesting stone, layered textures, and architectural details that give a home personality.” That interest in distinctive finishes comes with an eye toward longevity. Buyers aren't simply looking for a space that reflects the latest aesthetic, according to Wilder; they're considering how well its design will age. Loading... It's about creating a home that feels authentic to its architecture and will stand the test of time.” Neutral interiors get more personality Wilder also sees room for more individuality, although she cautions against interpreting that shift as a wholesale embrace of bright colors. "I don't necessarily think that means everyone suddenly wants brightly colored walls or really bold interiors. I think buyers are craving more personality and warmth,” she says of the move away from neutral, minimalist spaces. For some homes, that personality may come through in the finishes and fixtures rather than a dramatic change in wall color. “We're seeing people embrace richer wood finishes, beautiful tile, interesting lighting, and materials that make a home feel more collected and less cookie cutter,” she explains. “There's a difference between a home that's neutral and one that feels completely devoid of personality.” The key, in her view, is to let the property's architecture guide those choices instead of applying the same look to every home. “I always tell sellers that design should complement the architecture of the home. items.title: Massive Job Gains of 165,000 in October Bolster Case for More Fed Rate Hikes
items.description: Following a disappointing September , U.S. payrolls came roaring back in October as employers went on a hiring spree, adding 165,000 new jobs and pushing the unemployment rate down to 4.1%. The latest report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics , released Friday, shows nonfarm payroll growth more than doubled initial forecasts. These stronger-than-expected job figures increase the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will remain laser-focused on inflation and raise interest rates in the coming months. CME FedWatch currently prices a roughly 77% chance of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raising the federal funds to a 4%-4.25% range in December, followed by a 65% probability in January. " After last month’s hot inflation print put the next increase in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory, a soft jobs report was the one thing that could have complicated December," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel . "If Fed hawks were waiting to exhale, they can do so now." Work sectors that saw the strongest growth in October included professional and business services, which added 70,000 in jobs, well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the past 12 months. Health care came a distant second, with 42,000 payrolls added, followed by transportation and warehousing (+25,000 jobs), and manufacturing (+19,000). Meanwhile, the September employment data was revised up by 31,000 jobs, from +29,000 to +60,000, while the employment in August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 to +186,000. With these revisions, employment across these two months combined was 84,000 higher than previously reported. While calling the latest jobs data "impressive," Krimmel points out that the market is still in a low-hire, low-fire mode overall. However, he says that October's payroll surge could be signaling "some green shoots on the hiring side." "The numbers could still be revised, of course, and the trend matters more than any one point; but you don’t get a good trend without a good month," adds Krimmel. What this means for homebuyers For homebuyers, Krimmel says that a more dynamic labor market offers some support; however, to meaningfully improve Americans' purchasing power and boost demand requires wage growth to surpass inflation. Friday's jobs report showed nominal annual wage growth of 3.1% in October, trailing September's 3.7% inflation rate. "Nominal wage growth is necessary but not sufficient for real wage gains in this environment, so inflation has to come back down, too," says the economist. Loading... The major wildcard remains the ongoing war in Iran, which has driven up inflation and pushed mortgage rates above 7%. In this week's midterm elections this week, U.S. voters made it known that they were dissatisfied with the state of the economy by handing Democrats control of the House and Senate while flipping multiple traditional Republican strongholds, including Texas , South Carolina , and Kansas . Even so, Krimmel says that the results of the elections are unlikely to change much for the housing market in the short run. "Getting back to 'normal' in many metros takes more activity, which depends on improved buying power to bring buyers off the sidelines," he concludes. Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

items.title: Office Vacancy Eases in Q3 as New Supply Nears Record Lows
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Weekender | November 5, 2026 By: Amy Wolff Sorter Office Vacancy Eases in Q3 as New Supply Nears Record Lows The U.S. office market continued its recovery in Q3, according to national reports from CBRE , JLL , Cushman & Wakefield , Colliers and Lee & Associates . All reported lower vacancy year over year, new construction fell to its lowest level in decades, and demand continued to favor higher-quality buildings. Vacancy Declines Everywhere Colliers reported a 17.7% vacancy, representing a 60 basis-point decrease from the year before, and the lowest since Q4 2023. CBRE also noted a 60 bps drop, with vacancy at 18.2%; a fifth consecutive quarterly decline. Cushman & Wakefield had vacancy at 19.8%, down 30 bps from its Q3 2025 peak. JLL reported a vacancy of 21.5%, while Lee & Associates ended up at 13.8%, about 20 bps below its 2025 high. Leasing Favors the Best CBRE said leasing rose 4% year-over-year to 63.8 million square feet, the highest quarterly total since the fourth quarter of 2024, and expects 2026 leasing to surpass its 2022 record. JLL said leases signed over the past 12 months carried an average footprint increase of 13%, even as companies continue to downsize. All agreed that quality continued to drive demand. Cushman & Wakefield said Class A buildings accounted for two-thirds of third-quarter leasing, well above the 10-year average of 61%. Colliers pointed to demand from AI and tech occupiers. At the same time, Lee & Associates credited stricter attendance requirements at major financial firms and AI-driven startups in San Francisco and Silicon Valley, CA. Construction Pipeline Hits Bottom CBRE said completions fell 76% year-over-year to 1.5 million square feet, putting 2026 on track for the lowest annual total since the company started tracking in 1990. JLL said 9.6 million square feet were removed from inventory for conversions or redevelopment during the quarter; completions totaled 3.5 million square feet, and inventory has fallen by more than 45 million square feet since late 2023. Cushman & Wakefield said 23 million square feet is under construction, a 20% increase from its Q1 low, while CBRE reported a slight rise to 20.1 million square feet, driven largely by new starts in Manhattan and Miami, FL. Reports Split on Absorption Total The firms agreed on most Q3 metrics. But absorption figures depended greatly on who was counting. Colliers put positive absorption at 9.5 million square feet of positive net absorption, the ninth consecutive positive quarter. JLL reported the sixth straight positive quarter, citing 5 million square feet. CBRE noted absorption at 4.9 million square feet, representing the 10 th quarter of positive growth, while Cushman & Wakefield’s 50,000 square feet marked its fifth straight positive absorption. Lee & Associates said absorption was negative, ending four straight quarters of gains, with 70% of the shortfall involving Class B buildings. The Q4 Crystal Ball JLL expects interest rate volatility to slow some Q4 sales and delay lease decision-making. Still, tenant requirements in key markets are still above year-ago levels. At the same time, Cushman & Wakefield said a limited construction pipeline should help protect fundamentals from economic pressures. In contrast, Colliers said it anticipates a gradual improvement versus a broader recovery.
