items.title: Dallas Office Market on Rise
items.description: Dallas Office Market on Rise The Dallas-Fort Worth office market saw vacancy rates go down, while investment volume went up through the third quarter of 2026, according to Yardi Matrix data . Its competitive office pipeline was the second-largest in the country, while construction starts increased from their 2025 level. Dallas’ office investment volume reached $3.7 billion year-to-date through September, ranking third among the top 25 U.S. markets and second among its peers. The Metroplex trailed the Bay Area ($4.6 billion) and surpassed Houston ($2.1 billion), Austin ($1.6 billion) and Phoenix ($1.2 billion), among others. Dallas-Fort Worth’s office development pipeline included 3.6 million square feet of overall space across 23 projects at the end of September. The Metroplex led the peer set for construction activity. Metros that followed included Houston (2 million square feet) and the Bay Area (1.7 million square feet). Dallas’ office vacancy was down 360 basis points over the past 12 months. items.title: Workday Offers Up 140K SF Of Dublin HQ Despite Tightening Office Market
items.description: Courtesy of M&G Real Estate U.S. technology giant Workday is looking to sublease 140K SF of its new Dublin headquarters at College Square, The Irish Times reported . The space put back to the market is equivalent to approximately one-third of the 416K SF it committed to take at the development in April 2025 for its new European headquarters. It comprises three floors of approximately 47K SF each, all for immediate occupation. They have been made available individually or together, with flexible lease terms being offered. The company instructed adviser Cushman & Wakefield to market the space. Developed by Marlet Property Group and M&G Investments on the former Apollo House and College House sites, the 22-storey College Square consists of 540K SF of LEED Platinum office accommodation and 17K SF of retail space, alongside 58 apartments. The unexpected availability comes against a backdrop of improving office demand in Dublin and a potential space availability crunch last year. Office takeup in Q3 was 544K SF, bringing the total for the first nine months of 2026 to almost 1.5M SF, according to Knight Frank 's latest Dublin Office Market report. The agency has upgraded its full-year takeup forecast to 2.5M SF-2.6M SF from an earlier estimate of 2.2M SF-2.4M SF, putting activity on a par with 2025 and the 10-year average. Technology, media and telecoms companies accounted for 44% of Q3 leasing, with artificial intelligence businesses OpenAI and Klaviyo among the largest occupiers. OpenAI took 88K SF at Tropical Fruit Warehouse in Dublin 2, while Klaviyo leased 57K SF at One Le Pole Square in Dublin 8. And the supply outlook is becoming increasingly challenging. Dublin's overall office vacancy rate fell to 12.7% in Q3, down from 13.7% at the start of the year, while prime rents remained at €65 to €67.50 per SF — though Knight Frank expects prime rents to reach €70 per SF by the end of 2026, with pre-let rents potentially reaching €75 per SF. Seventy-two percent of new space already delivered or due to be delivered by 2027 is pre-let, according to Knight Frank. “Adding space that is reserved, the amount taken increases to 78%. This makes the case for the commencement of new office development even more compelling,” Knight Frank Chief Economist and Research Director Joan Henry said in the report. “Developers or investors who take on the challenge to commence new office developments will deliver into a market in 2028/2029 that needs new space to keep Ireland in its leading position as an attractive location for global business,” she added. items.title: Housing affordability improves quarterly, annually in Houston
items.description: Housing affordability improves quarterly, annually in Houston by Emily Marek November 06, 2026 The typical monthly mortgage payment — including principal, taxes and insurance — decreased to $2,520 in Houston during the third quarter. (via HAR) Forty-two percent of Houston-area households could afford a median-priced home during the third quarter, according to the Houston Association of REALTORS ’® new Housing and Rental Affordability Report. That was up from 40% a quarter ago and 39% during the third quarter of 2025. Single-family affordability Despite a higher average 30-year fixed mortgage rate , median home prices declined 0.4% year over year to $340,300. That meant the typical monthly mortgage payment — including principal, taxes and insurance — decreased to $2,520, down from $2,510 a year ago and $2,550 in Q2. Given that cost, Houston households needed an annual income of at least $100,800 to afford a median-priced home. Forty-two percent fell into that income range. “ Affordability is moving in the right direction, and that’s encouraging, but we also know many consumers are still concerned about the cost of buying a home, particularly with mortgage rates remaining elevated,” said HAR Chair Theresa Hill . “For buyers who may have been sitting on the sidelines, it’s worth taking another look at what’s possible. A Realtor can help buyers understand their options and determine what’s realistic for their budget.” Statewide, 45% of households could afford a median-priced home ($335,000) in the third quarter, up from 42% a year prior; nationally, 38% could afford the median of $432,900, which was up from $426,800 a year ago. Rental affordability Among Houston’s single-family rental properties, 44% of households could afford the median lease price in the third quarter. That was down from 45% in both the third quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026. The median monthly lease cost was $2,195, down from $2,200 a year prior. That meant households needed an annual income of $87,800 to afford a single-family rental, down from $88,000 last year. items.title: BLS: U.S. Economy Unexpectedly Adds 165,000 Jobs in October
items.description: BLS: U.S. Economy Unexpectedly Adds 165,000 Jobs in October by Abby Cox November 6, 2026 November 6, 2026 6 WASHINGTON, D.C. — Total nonfarm employment in the United States increased by 165,000 jobs in October, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). The figure shows an unexpected increase from the upwardly revised +60,000 in September, and far above the 59,000 figure projected by Dow Jones economists, according to CNBC . The unemployment rate nudged down to 4.1 percent, compared to the forecasted 4.2 percent. In addition, August’s number increased by 53,000, raising the total to 186,000, while September revisions increased by 31,000. With these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 percent higher than previously reported. October job gains mostly occurred in professional and business services (+70,000), well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. The sector has also added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 2025. Employment continued to trend up in professional, scientific and technical services (+33,000), administrative and support and waste management and remediation services (+28,000) and in management of companies and enterprises (+9,000). Healthcare added 42,000 jobs in October, which is higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the prior 12 months. Employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home healthcare services (+11,000) and outpatient care centers (+5,000). Transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) contributing most of the gain. The manufacturing sector continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 since a low in December 2025. Job gains occurred in computer and electronic product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000) and primary metal manufacturing (+4,000). Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries including mining, quarrying, and oil-and-gas extraction, construction, wholesale trade, retail trade, information, financial activities, social assistance, leisure and hospitality and government. items.title: Dallas Dodgeball Tournament Raises $200K To Fight Child Homelessness
items.description: Live Poll DALLAS, Texas (August 26, 2026) -- Dodge For A Cause, a high-energy corporate dodgeball tournament, returned to SMU's Moody Coliseum on Wednesday, August 26, drawing 28 spirited teams to compete for bragging rights in support of Vogel, a Dallas nonprofit dedicated to helping children and families overcome homelessness and poverty. Varsity Brands, competing as "Varsity Blues & Bruisers" clinched the championship title, while last year's champion, Sewell Automotive Companies competing as "The Dodgefather's VIII," claimed second place. The biggest win of the night, however, came off the court: the tournament raised $200,000 to support Vogel's mission. This year's event was supported by Kainos Capital, Varsity Brands, Copart, Kirkland & Ellis, and many more. Dallas boasts the sixth-largest GDP in the nation and is home to more than 20 Fortune 500 headquarters, yet the city faces a sobering reality: nearly one in three children in Dallas grow up in poverty, one of the highest child poverty rates among large U.S. cities. Vogel works to break this cycle by ensuring every child has a safe home, a self-sufficient family, and the foundation for long-term success in school and life. The organization provides developmental programs for children and supports parents in building stable, nurturing home environments. For families across Dallas, Dodge For A Cause means more than just a night of dodgeball: it's a step toward a stronger, more hopeful future. Since 1987, Vogel has seen over 17,000 young, homeless children walk through their doors. Vogel provides educational, developmental, and therapeutic services to children and families affected by homelessness. Using its "Two-Generational" approach to solving homelessness, services are provided to client families through the early childhood education program and parent opportunity department. items.title: RealPRO Select helps lift Realtor.com revenue
items.description: Move , the parent company of Realtor.com , said the momentum generated by RealPRO Select in fiscal year 2026 has carried over into the first quarter of fiscal year 2027. During the first quarter of FY 2027, Realtor.com recorded $160 million in revenue, up 5% year over year, marking the segment’s eighth consecutive quarter of growth. These financial results were highlighted during News Corp ’s fiscal year 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call on Wednesday evening. “In a housing market constrained by 7%-plus mortgage rates , Damian [Eales] and the team have exhibited exceptional discipline in their operational focus and AI integration, and that approach has converted revenue growth into meaningful bottom-line expansion,” Robert Thomson, the CEO of News Corp, said during the earnings call. RealPRO Select grows News Corp executives attributed Realtor.com ’s strong revenue performance to the growth of RealPRO Select. The company said it is focused on enhancing the platform with stronger lead generation, branding, productivity tools and training capabilities. Realtor.com also focused on the expansion of RealAssist AI during Q1, including the launch of a pilot of RealAssist in Rich Communication Services (RCS), integrated directly into Google search and available on iOS and Android. “The pilot is already attracting new users, driving strong engagement, and helping us capture pre-search intent earlier in the buyer journey before consumers ever enter a browser,” Damian Eales, the CEO of Move, wrote in a blog post about the company's quarterly performance. In addition, Realtor.com also launched RealAssist AI for Realtor.com+, which Eales said helps agents onboard their clients faster, build more tailored searches, summarize client activity and draft follow-ups in their own voice. “The platform is already supporting thousands of successful agent-client connections, and early feedback on these AI tools has been very positive,” Eales wrote. Other highlights Eales also highlighted the relaunch of the My Home dashboard, which now includes a collaboration with Opendoor . Eales said this is encouraging sellers to engage a listing agent much earlier in their journey. In addition, News Corp also noted that Comscore data shows 4.9 visits per unique user to Realtor.com, up 8% annually, and an average of 263 million monthly visits in the quarter, which the company said represents a “substantial” lead over Redfin and Homes.com . Despite these strong numbers, Realtor.com noted that lead volume was down 11%, which the portal attributed to broader market conditions and its repositioning of customer acquisitions to higher-quality and higher-value leads. “Despite a constrained housing market , Realtor.com’s strategy is delivering positive results, and we’re well positioned to grow as conditions improve,” Eales wrote. “Our focus remains on investing in our audience and AI tools that enhance a consumer’s experience and augment the role of the professional agent.” Overall, News Corp’s digital real estate services segment generated $529 million in revenue, up 10% from a year prior. items.title: American Housing Corp names leadership for new Austin division
items.description: The American Housing Corporation launched an Austin homebuilding division and named three industry veterans to lead the new operation as it ramps up an infill-focused, prefabricated rowhome platform, the company announced this week. Austin is the launch market for the company’s infill homebuilding strategy, which centers on designing, manufacturing and constructing urban rowhomes. The move comes as builders look for ways to add “missing middle” housing in supply-constrained, high-cost markets without relying solely on traditional greenfield development. Parker Scott, a former division president at LGI Homes , was appointed general manager, Daniel Green will serve as director of construction operations and Luke Allen will serve as director of land. Scott brings more than 20 years of homebuilding sales and operational experience to the role. Green joins from senior construction positions at Homebound , ATCO Structures and Perry Homes , where he focused on building operations and execution systems. Allen, who previously held land roles at Lennar and Ashton Woods , will oversee land acquisition, underwriting and pipeline development for the Austin market. In October 2026, American Housing Corp completed its “Demo 2” prototype using a componentized, prefabricated building system. The company is building a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant in Southeast Austin designed to produce up to 1,200 homes annually, according to the announcement. The factory-scale approach is intended to standardize production, shorten build times and provide more cost certainty, which could appeal to capital providers and municipalities looking for scalable infill housing solutions. For real estate investors and lenders, the combination of an infill land strategy with a controlled-offsite construction environment could change underwriting assumptions around cycle times and construction risk. Alongside the Austin division launch, the company restructured its real estate operations and parted ways with co-founder Bobby Fijan. The firm credited Fijan with helping establish its early real estate footprint and championing urban, family-sized housing. Related More: homebuilder Texas

items.title: Meet the 27-Year-Old Who’s Trying To Bring Housing Back to Rural Ohio
items.description: When it comes to the hottest locations that attract young 20-somethings, Mansfield, OH , probably isn't the first place that comes to mind. For years, Mansfield’s nickname was “The Fun Center of Ohio ” because of its family-friendly attractions and its status in the 1970s as a mini-bike manufacturing hub. More recently, the town of 47,000, located halfway between Columbus and Cleveland , earned the local nickname of “Danger City” after the Westinghouse electric plant left in 1990 and the town fell into deep economic decline. That didn’t stop Ben Goehner . The 27-year-old serial entrepreneur, who started a painting and landscaping business as a teenager, relocated to Mansfield from Seattle a year ago, hoping to revitalize rural housing through his vertically integrated housing development company, Western Dominion Land . Vertical integration is a development model in which a single company controls the full life cycle of a housing project. “In other countries, they’ve figured out that vertically integrating construction means you’re not paying a margin out to every single step," Goehner explains. "If you own the system—from a lumberyard, to producing panels or modular, to buying the land, to developing the land, to building the homes—you're not paying everyone’s markup along the way, and you can actually deliver that home at a reasonable price.” Goehner is building a factory in Mansfield to produce structured panels that he says will cut single-family home construction from months to weeks and allow him to charge much less than other builders. The first panels are expected to roll off the production line in early 2027. Currently, it takes 8.8 months to construct a home from start to finish, according to the National Association of Home Builders . Goehner says his process allows a home to be built and move-in-ready in 40 days. Western Dominion has already built about 500 housing units across Ohio, starting at $200,000 for a single-family home. Western Dominion focuses on what it calls "attainable housing"—homes priced below what the median household income in the area can afford but not income-limited, meaning they work for the vast majority of families and buyers. In Mansfield, where the median listing price is $229,000, he says, "single-family homes at $215,000 sold instantly. At $260,000, they sat for months." Loading... Ben Goehner says rural housing development has been sorely overlooked by large-scale developers. Ben Goehner As he sees it, 25% of the homes on the market are priced for 60% to 70% of buyers, while the rest of what’s being built is at the top end of the market. Furthermore, only 8% of construction happens in rural areas, despite 20% of the population living there. "The government is too focused on low-income housing" and low-income housing tax credits, he says. “And the last few housing bills they passed were only structured to deliver essentially more urban multifamily units and incentivize builders to build more low-income housing with tax credits." In rural communities, he adds, “We have a terrible amount of aged housing inventory. Most of our homes are from before 1970, which would be fine if it didn't cost so much to remodel. “From the '90s to the 2000s, we’re building a good amount of homes. As a country, we were doing about 1.6 million a year. And then in rural America, we were doing about 220,000 homes a year. And then 2008 hits, and that drops down to about 60,000 homes a year in rural America." Along the way, smaller builders disappeared, and larger builders were disincentivized from building in rural areas because of the red tape involved. "If you want to build in rural America and you go to a bank, unless you have all the cash, you have to show comps," he says. "You've got to be, like, ‘All right, we think these homes are going to sell for this much because these guys sold for this much.' And if no one's built for five to 50 years, which is the case in a lot of these communities, that can be difficult." The added costs of building in rural areas, like having to pull utilities, "mean you're spending $25,000 to $50,000 per lot before you can even start putting a house on it or connecting your utilities to the lot." Since the COVID-19 pandemic, home prices in rural communities have risen sharply. A Realtor.com® housing analysis of home prices from November 2019 to November 2025 found that median listing prices increased more than 70% in rural counties while in-metro counties saw home prices increase around 30% during the same time period. "A lot of the politicians we talk to, they go, 'I didn't know that that county needed housing. I didn't know rural needed housing because the population is shrinking.' But then when you look at why the population is shrinking, it's because they haven't gotten any new homes for 20 to 40 years." "You've got this huge demand. But on paper, on the surface, it looks like there's no demand because the population's declining," he continues. "And that's how you get cities like Holiday City." Loading... One of Western Dominion's attainable properties Western Dominion Land Co. Holiday City , near the Ohio border with Indiana and Michigan , has a population of just 48 people, but it is home to three large businesses—Chase Brass & Copper Co., 20/20 Custom Molded Products, and a Menards Distribution Center—which draw around 1,500 commuters from out of state. "Let's put up, you know, 300 homes, and a portion of the workforce can actually stop commuting an hour or two every day," Goehner says. Goehner hopes Ohio's new slate of elected officials will help advance rural building by offsetting some of the infrastructure-related costs of building in rural areas. In exchange, he would sell homes at his “attainable” housing rates. "The government needs to stop spending thousands of dollars a month per unit to subsidize rents when they could simply spend a little bit upfront to make it viable to build at a reasonable price point again," he says. items.title: This Glass Barn Redefines Modern Country Living—and It’s Fully Furnished
items.description: An eye-catching glass barn with a 28-foot great room in New Hope, PA , is now being offered fully furnished for $5.5 million. Built in 1987 and originally designed by Richard Olcott and Todd Schliemann of Polshek & Partners, the four-bedroom Bucks County home with an attached two-car garage was entirely reimagined in 2020. “From the inside and out, the wall of glass and enormous foyer are a remarkable statement,” says listing agent Ali Jankowski of Kurfiss Sotheby’s International Realty . “It’s a special and spectacular home in all ways.” Loading... items.title: How One Real Estate Investor Replaced Evictions With a $5,000-a-Month Sober Living Business
items.description: Five years into his real-estate investing journey, Hunter Foote grew disillusioned. Starting in 2010, he had flipped a few homes and purchased several multi-family units. The cash flow was solid, but the tenants made his life challenging. “I have a long history of being frustrated and evicting tenants and dealing with some folks who weren’t at the best time of their lives,” he says. He wanted to provide housing and help people, but evictions were not only costly, but disheartening. He wasn’t sure he could continue. Cue Thanksgiving 2015. His sister-in-law works in the recovery space as a program manager in central Connecticut . In talking about her work, Foote says, “she was in tears about how folks who get out of treatment have nowhere to go.” Loading... Hunter Foote bought homes primarily in New England, where he learned which towns have more lenient permitting. Vanderburgh Sober Living People get sober but haven’t yet made sober friends who can provide a couch to surf or room to rent. The person’s family typically wants them to have more time clean before they welcome them home or lend financial support. The end result is that many people find themselves sober but without housing options. Foote was intrigued, and liked the idea of helping people while still investing in real estate. “I’m a bit of a nerd and spent a year doing research,” he says. The problem was that, back then, there was no infrastructure to guide someone in starting a sober-living home. “It was the Wild West with people calling it different names and everyone was doing different things,” he adds. In 2016, he bought a seven-bedroom home for $360,000 in Worcester, MA . The home was zoned as a two-family unit with six bedrooms upstairs and a basement apartment that, combined, “didn’t fit the bill for a lot of investors.” It had been listed for $480,000 but had sat on the market for more than 200 days, which is how Foote picked it up at a discount. He used hard money to buy the property at 12% interest with two points. He had 12 months to either pay off the loan or figure out financing–eventually refinancing out using a DSCR loan. Getting the property fixed up and furnished was easy. Getting the beds filled, less so. “Everyone says there is just demand everywhere,” he says. “But to get the right people, you really need to work hard.” Loading... The living room of one of Foote's sober living homes. Vanderburgh Sober Living He had to network quickly, meeting with people from jail pre-release programs, drug courts and treatment centers. “You have to get your name out there to get the right referrals. The key to success is getting the right people in there in the first place.” It took six months to break even. At nine months, he was profitable. Once the home was operating at capacity, it generated around $13,000 in monthly revenue. Operating expenses totaled roughly $4,000, leaving $9,000 in net operating income. After accounting for property taxes, insurance and the mortgage, the home netted approximately $5,000 a month. Sober living isn’t just about “filling the beds.” The average stay is between six and nine months. However, that doesn’t account for the folks who leave after “three weeks, three days or three hours.” Sometimes men are dropped off and only committed to sober living so that jail or the recovery program would release them–the person never had any intention of staying clean and committing to a sober house. “They stay until the car drives away, and then all they think about is that they are free,” Foote says. Others “didn’t think the rules would apply” to them. Still others have drug paraphernalia in their bags that’s discovered during the check-in bag search. “These guys try to tell me marijuana is legal in Massachusetts ,” he says. “It is, but it’s not allowed in a sober living house.” In the beginning, Foote was losing money every time someone committed and then dropped out. He has learned he has to charge a $200 nonrefundable fee to cover the intake process, which includes a drug screening and bag search. It’s just one of the systems he has learned in his 10 years of owning about 10 sober-living homes and managing many more. Foote bought homes primarily in New England, where he learned which towns have more lenient permitting. Worcester was “one of the toughest” cities to operate in because it required additional features in the home. “They made us put in sprinklers and extra fire alarms that other cities weren’t requiring,” he says. Foote’s homes are NARR Level II certified recovery residences, which means there is no paid staff on site. Each home houses only one gender, and the home has a house mentor who lives there for free in exchange for helping manage the day-to-day. These days, Foote spends less time managing his own rentals, and more time helping others with theirs. “We transitioned out of running homes so that we could launch some software offerings” to help others in the sober living space. They’re in the process of launching a software called Sober Desk that helps sober-living landlords manage their homes. For example, this software helps homeowners collect weekly rent, a common practice in the sober-living space. “Logging the drug screens is also not something you can do in Buildium” for example. He has also launched a management company, Vanderburgh Sober Living , to help run other people’s sober-living homes. His company also assists investors with finding the right property and launching. When it comes to choosing a house, “the bigger, the better” but location dictates what works. For example, in Texas , “there are so many inexpensive four-bedroom homes” where “eight beds in four bedrooms” can work really well. items.title: ‘The American Dream Has an Address’—and Both Parties Are on Notice, Strategists Say
items.description: Democrats' historic midterm sweep will hand them control of Congress, but keeping it could depend on whether they can make housing more affordable , according to leading strategists from both parties. "The American dream has an address," veteran Democratic strategist Donna Brazile told a room of real estate professionals in New Orleans on Saturday. Speaking alongside conservative political strategist Shermichael Singleton at the National Association of Realtors®' NAR NXT conference , Brazile cautioned that Democrats' electoral victories were not an unconditional endorsement of their policies, but a demand for relief from the rising cost of living. Singleton agreed, arguing that Republicans had already learned that lesson the hard way. "Our voters felt we fundamentally failed," he said, pointing to rising fuel and food costs as well as younger Americans' inability to afford homes as examples of the administration's unfulfilled affordability promises. Brazile warned that Democrats could face the same reckoning in 2028 if they fail to act. "If you're not going to help build more houses and take care of the affairs of the American people, they will kick our [expletive] in two years," she said. Housing affordability becomes an electoral reckoning The affordability crisis that helped propel Democrats to victory Tuesday had been a liability for their own party just two years earlier—a fact that Brazile said is a warning to both parties heading into 2028. "Affordability has been on the minds of American people now for two consecutive years," Brazile said, acknowledging that Joe Biden and Kamala Harris had failed to recognize the depth of voters' frustration ahead of the 2024 election. And today, housing offers perhaps the clearest illustration of why that frustration has persisted. Mortgage rates climbed from roughly 3% in 2021 to nearly 8% by late 2023, compounding a pandemic-era surge in home prices, Lawrence Yun , chief economist at the National Association of Realtors, explained during a separate presentation Saturday. And while borrowing costs have since eased, home prices continue to climb. Prices rose in approximately 78% of U.S. metropolitan markets during the third quarter of 2026, according to NAR's latest quarterly report . Existing homeowners have benefited from that appreciation, with Yun estimating that the typical owner has gained nearly $200,000 in housing wealth since before the pandemic. Prospective buyers, meanwhile, face a considerably higher cost of entry. The consequences are particularly stark for younger Americans. First-time buyers now account for just 22% of home purchases, while their median age has reached 40, matching last year's record high, according to NAR's newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers . "Maybe the election result was partly reflecting that fact," Yun said, pointing to younger Americans struggling to enter the housing market. For Singleton, 36, the frustration is personal. "You do everything right. You get the college degree. You get the graduate degree. You start the family. You can't afford anything," he said. Singleton purchased his first home at 28, but said many of his friends, now approaching or entering their 40s, still can’t afford to buy. And with millennials and Gen Z now accounting for a substantial share of the electorate, Singleton argued that housing access could become a more decisive factor in how younger Americans vote. Loading... Political strategists Donna Brazile and Shermichael Singleton joined moderators at the National Association of Realtors' Federal Legislative and Political Forum in New Orleans on Saturday to discuss the 2026 midterm elections and their implications for housing policy. Loading... “We got to give more Americans a lifeline and a path to homeownership," Brazile said. "That's the bottom line.” A bipartisan opening—but can Washington deliver? Amid deep political divisions, Brazile and Singleton's agreement on the urgency of the housing crisis was striking. And already, there's a powerful precedent for cooperation on the issue. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act , enacted in July, received overwhelming support from both parties, passing the Senate 85-5 and the House 358-32. The legislation aims to boost supply by reducing regulatory barriers, expanding financing opportunities, and supporting new approaches to construction. But passage was only the first step. Many provisions still require implementation or funding, and their effects on the market could take years to materialize. Singleton sees opportunities to build on that foundation by addressing barriers closer to home, including local permitting delays, construction costs, and tariffs on Canadian lumber . "One of the things that I hear about often from them is that the length of time it takes to get something approved is very costly," he said, referring to conversations with builders. He also proposed investing in training younger Americans as electricians, plumbers, and other skilled tradespeople to help build the millions of homes the country needs. It's an idea echoed by Scott Norman , CEO of the Texas Association of Builders, who identified workforce development as a bipartisan priority in an exclusive interview with Realtor.com following Democrats' sweep of the state's elected offices. "The more folks we can get in the business, that'll drive down those labor costs," Norman said. Brazile, meanwhile, said Democrats' affordability agenda places housing alongside groceries, energy, and family expenses, with an emphasis on cutting red tape and expanding supply. "Affordability, affordability, affordability. It's not a slogan that Democrats can use again unless they do something about it," she said. items.title: 220-Unit Mixed-Use Project Moves Forward Near Rowan University
items.description: Hundreds of new apartments have been approved on a former industrial site in the center of a South Jersey college town. Google Maps 220 Rowan Blvd., another Nexus Properties project in Glassboro The Glassboro Planning Board voted Wednesday to greenlight Nexus Properties ’ plans for 220 units and about 8K SF of retail on the corner of Academy and East High streets in the town's central business district, 42Freeway reported . The market-rate project, dubbed Glassworks, will span two city blocks and six stories on a site about three-quarters of a mile from the core of Rowan University’s campus. Nexus expects the project to deliver sometime in 2029, 70and73 reported . Its new retail component will effectively be a replacement for older commercial properties that existed on the site. The site once housed the Whitney Glass Works, which closed in the 1920s. The Heritage Glass Museum operates in the neighborhood and will remain open, alongside Angelo’s Diner. The former Glassboro Library is set to be razed. Lawrenceville-based Nexus is also a major student housing owner in Glassboro, with five properties listed on its website. Some of those are part of the Rowan Boulevard project, where Nexus struck up a $425M public-private partnership with Rowan University to build a mixed-use neighborhood overlooking the campus. While permitting can be a challenge in South Jersey, the region is seeing some multifamily development, a large share of which is affordable housing meant to meet state requirements for municipalities under the Mount Laurel doctrine. Enforcement of the 1975 New Jersey Supreme Court decision requiring local governments to use zoning to further attainable housing production was clarified in 2024. That push is also underway in Voorhees, where 180 affordable units are on the way. Administrators there greenlit plans for a 178-unit, market-rate office-to-residential conversion last month. But mixed-use plans for a redevelopment of the nearby Echelon Mall have fallen through since they were introduced last year, the Philadelphia Business Journal reported this week. Hoboken Brownstone Co . told the outlet this was due to uncertainty about a $90M tax credit it sought through New Jersey’s Aspire program, which has paused its application process. items.title: Bank Reportedly Looking To Sell $500M In Data Center Loans Following Elections
items.description: Dutch Bank ING is reportedly seeking buyers for roughly $500M of data center loans, an unusual move that comes as fears mount that Democratic gains in the U.S. midterm elections could derail data center projects across the country. WikimediaCommons/Someone Not Awful The bank is accepting offers for 12 loans through a process known as bids wanted in competition, Bloomberg reports . Bids on the debt are due later this month, with individual offers required to exceed $10M. The loans being offered include $25M of debt backing Project Jupiter, the 1,400-acre New Mexico campus being developed by Blue Owl-backed Stack Infrastructure for OpenAI , Oracle and SoftBank 's Stargate initiative. The potentially 2.45-gigawatt project had faced concerns about possible delays before ING began marketing this debt — in September, Oracle sent developers a force majeure notice that would allow it to defer payments if the project is delayed or derailed. ING is also reportedly looking to sell debt tied to data centers being developed by major operators like Vantage and CyrusOne . The Dutch lender is a significant player in data center financing, having been involved in more than 200 deals globally. The auction is reportedly among the first to involve a portfolio made up exclusively of data center debt, and it comes as global markets are reassessing the risks surrounding U.S. data center development following the midterms. Democrats won gubernatorial races in states such as Texas, Georgia and Pennsylvania where data centers became a key campaign issue. According to market research firm Cleanview , about 40% of planned data center capacity in the U.S. is in states where newly elected governors have called for a pause to data center construction. The shifting political winds also extend to Washington, D.C., where Democrats’ control of both chambers of Congress has industry leaders bracing for more aggressive oversight and new restrictions on a sector already struggling to build fast enough to meet demand. Wall Street has reacted accordingly . The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4% on Thursday, its worst day since 2020, as investors sold stocks tied to the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. The index gained back about 1.5% on Friday. The bond markets also experienced major declines in the price of structured debt tied to AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Galaxy Digital. items.title: How a new Pulte Florida agrihood makes conservation a buyer desire
items.description: For years, Central Florida’s exploding population growth and rapidly expanding suburban sprawl have clashed with local efforts to protect the region’s dwindling green space and undeveloped land. PulteGroup ’s new 1,200-acre community on Orlando's eastern edge aims to balance these seemingly contradictory interests. The community is called The Grow . Once undeveloped, rural land, the property is set to begin morphing into a roughly 2,200-home “agrihood” centered around a 9-acre working farm. In keeping with its conservation focus, the plan calls for reserving just over half of the site from development, including wetlands, conservation areas and shared green space. The Grow offers a potential case study in balancing growth and conservation, a tension deeply felt in Central Florida and many other high-growth Sun Belt markets. Between 2000 and 2025, the Orlando metro area’s population grew nearly 80%, from 1.64 million to 2.95 million. That growth reshaped once-rural communities on the region’s edges, replacing undeveloped land with new subdivisions, apartments and shopping centers. Many long-time Sunshine State residents now lament the loss of “Old Florida,” marked by a landscape of open land, working ranches and orange groves that are now developed. When Pulte, the sole homebuilder at The Grow, purchased the community’s lots in 2023, it set out to build a premier community that responded to these tensions. "One of our biggest selling features is the openness of the community and how much greenery we left. Everywhere you look, you're surrounded by trees,” Patrick McNamara, a Sales Manager at Pulte, told HousingWire TBD . However, the true distinguisher between The Grow and other local communities will be its working farm, a rare amenity that carries the conservation theme beyond protecting land to putting it to use. For Pulte, which held a grand opening for the community in late September, the farm and the extensive conservation space give the builder a way to stand out to prospective homebuyers, a crucial edge considering the challenging sales environment homebuilders are facing. The Grow will feature a nine-acre working farm, along with two smaller, resident-only farms. (Photo courtesy of The Grow) How the agrihood will work in practice The working farm is central to the community’s agrihood concept – providing fresh, sustainably grown produce. items.title: Massachusetts AG issues rule on shared appreciation mortgages, NCLC calls for broader protections
items.description: The Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office has implemented a new rule governing shared appreciation mortgages, adding disclosure and consumer protection requirements for a niche home equity product that has faced recent scrutiny. The rule, effective Nov. 6, clarifies when nonprofit shared appreciation mortgage (SAM) lenders are shielded from state consumer protection claims and sets new notice standards, including prominent disclosure of the maximum amount borrowers may have to repay, according to an announcement from the National Consumer Law Center ( NCLC ). The regulation stems from a provision in the state’s economic development bill , passed in November 2024. That statute carved out a broad waiver of liability under Massachusetts consumer protection laws for certain nonprofit SAMs, including loans originated by BlueHub Capital . Advocates say the legislative change created a “dangerous loophole” that exposed distressed homeowners to complex and costly loan structures with limited recourse. Under the BlueHub-style model, borrowers typically receive a fixed-rate first mortgage alongside a second lien tied to future home price appreciation . The SAM second lien requires the homeowner to share a portion of any increase in property value with the lender upon sale, transfer or refinance. Because the payoff amount is variable and not set in dollars at origination, borrowers can face unexpectedly large balloon payments when they attempt to exit the loan. NCLC noted that the risks of these structures have been highlighted in Humes v. BlueHub Capital Inc. , a Massachusetts class-action lawsuit alleging SAMs embed hidden, subprime-level costs that can strip significant equity and accelerate home loss. The court found BlueHub liable for violating multiple state lending laws and recently certified the class to move forward, according to NCLC. “While presented as a lifeline, shared appreciation mortgages often become a trap,” Andrea Bopp Stark, senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center, said in a statement. “The AG’s final rule protects people from BlueHub’s loan model and similar products, but Massachusetts must go further to prevent harm from more common home equity theft loan products, including Home Equity Investment Loans.” Will rules eventually extend to HEIs? The AG’s new rule does not eliminate SAMs but seeks to ensure that nonprofit and other lenders using these instruments do so transparently and within defined consumer protection boundaries. The regulation spells out the limited circumstances in which a SAM lender can be insulated from claims under Massachusetts consumer protection law and establishes a framework for robust disclosures, including clear presentation of the maximum possible repayment obligation. While praising the change, NCLC argues that the rule does not reach a far enough to impact a growing category of products — home equity investments (HEIs). These provide upfront cash to a homeowner in exchange for a share of the future home price appreciation. NCLC characterized these arrangements as high risk for borrowers, as the actual amount owed depends on home price growth and triggers large, lump-sum obligations. A representative at the AG's office did not immediately respond to HousingWire 's request for comment on the changes. Massachusetts AG Andrea Joy Campbell has already challenged one HEI provider, Hometap . The state alleges consumer protection violations tied to HEI structures. But NCLC noted that the latest rulemaking in Massachusetts does not specifically regulate HEI products. “The new rules provide important safeguards and requirements for SAMs, and stronger and broader rules are needed to address the high-risk HEI loans that are now targeting Massachusetts homeowners,” Bopp Stark said. Legal and regulatory efforts elsewhere Consumers in other parts of the country have challenged HEI providers in court. Last year, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a 2023 judgment from a district court in Washington state, ruling that Unison 's HEI product amounted to a reverse mortgage under state law. In August, HEI provider Unlock settled with the Office of the Minnesota Attorney General over allegations that the company’s home equity agreements (HEAs) were mortgage loans that violated state usury caps, disclosure rules and licensing requirements. Companies say they are supportive of regulatory efforts, pointing to a legal framework passed earlier this year in Illinois that could serve as model at the national level. At the Mortgage Bankers Association 's Annual Convention & Expo last month, executives at Point told HousingWire they believe universal regulations are coming . “We believe that these companies are going to be regulated,” said Dan McPheeters, Point's head of business development and partnerships. “The practical effect is, it’s difficult to comply with [mortgage regulations] for a product that doesn’t have a monthly payment, that isn’t self-amortizing. … That said, as long as you address those tactical issues, this should be regulated.” The NCLC urges additional state action to close what they see as remaining gaps in oversight of shared appreciation equity-based mortgage products. Their recommendations include: Clarifying that all SAMs and HEIs are mortgage loans subject to federal and state mortgage laws and regulations Requiring contractual repayment caps set at reasonable statutory limits Requiring borrowers to meet with independent legal counsel or a HUD-certified housing counselor before closing Prohibiting overly restrictive provisions around occupancy , maintenance and use of the home Allowing homeowners to bring direct legal claims against predatory lenders Related More: Home Equity Investments Massachusetts National Consumer Law Center

items.title: Elizabeth Warren expected to lead Senate banking committee in January
items.description: Sen. Elizabeth Warren is expected to become chair of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs when Democrats take control of Congress in January, giving the Massachusetts Democrat expanded authority to investigate financial institutions and advance legislation affecting the sector. The move is expected as a result of this week's midterm elections, which saw both the Senate and House of Representatives flip from Republican to Democratic majorities. Several outlets, including The Wall Street Journal and Reuters, anticipate that Warren is lined up for the role, even though other senators could theoretically rank ahead of her for the chairmanship. The transition would give Warren, who is currently a ranking member of the legislative committee, more staff and subpoena powers, potentially increasing scrutiny of major banks, consumer lenders, private equity firms and cryptocurrency companies. Warren, who would replace current Chairman Tim Scott (R-S.C.), is also expected to examine the Trump administration's mass firings of financial regulatory employees and potential conflicts of interest involving companies with ties to the president. Warren has built her political career around financial regulation and consumer protection. A former Harvard University law professor and bankruptcy expert, she became involved in developing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in the wake of the great financial crisis under President Barack Obama before winning a Senate seat in 2012. Her expected chairmanship comes as the CFPB faces significant operational challenges and restructuring under the Trump administration, a move that she has publicly criticized. The administration, meanwhile, has argued that the CFPB over-regulates consumer lenders and has been used to target political opponents and disfavored industries, going so far as to scale back enforcements this year. The CFPB has undergone a leadership shuffle as a result of the administration's efforts to scale back the agency's power. In September, the committee advanced the nomination of Brian Johnson, Trump’s newest nominee to become director of the bureau, a move that Warren opposed. Related More: CFPB Elizabeth Warren Senate

items.title: NAR President Kevin Brown warns of outside forces threatening real estate marketplace
items.description: As his term as president of the National Association of Realtors (NAR) comes to a close, Kevin Brown is warning real estate professionals that outside forces seeking greater control of the industry could threaten the transparency and competition that are the backbone of the current real estate marketplace. In remarks prepared for NAR NXT in New Orleans this week, Brown drew parallels between the forces that contributed to the 2008 housing crisis and those he believes are now attempting to reshape how real estate is bought and sold. "Today, outside forces have once again entered our industry, and this time around it is our marketplace instead of our financial system, motivated by profits, control and market share," Brown said. He did not identify the companies or organizations he was referring to, but his comments come as the industry debates the future of listing distribution , broker control of listing data and the role of multiple listing services (MLSs). Defending the MLS system Brown said he believes the MLS system remains essential to maintaining competition and giving buyers and sellers access to comprehensive property information. "America is home to the fairest, most accessible and transparent real estate market in the world," Brown said. "That is because of a pro-competitive foundation that provides the broadest, most reliable view of the market, anchored in the MLS system." Perhaps in a nod to the increase in private listings , he emphasized that consumer choice depends not only on the ability to make decisions but also on access to the information needed to make them. "A fair and transparent marketplace gives homebuyers and sellers both choice and clarity — the freedom to choose and the information to understand the consequences of that choice," he said. According to Brown, NAR is working with MLSs, associations and industry leaders to address marketplace concerns while advocating for the MLS system in Washington . He also urged members to take a more active role in defending the existing marketplace. "Be prepared to support and defend a marketplace that doesn’t just benefit a select few, but a marketplace that serves us all — the consumer, the industry and Realtors," Brown said. NAR must be willing to change When it comes to the association, Brown acknowledged shortcomings. "If NAR wants to lead change, we must be willing to change ourselves," Brown said. "We cannot wait for outside forces to set our agenda or determine our direction." Brown pointed to organizational changes this year, including staff reductions, streamlined governance and a renewed focus on member services. These changes are part of NAR's three-year strategic plan , which focuses on rebuilding the member experience and modernizing the association. "That is why we have rightsized our staff, streamlined our governance structure and sharpened our focus," he said. "But the real test is not whether we created a plan. It is whether that plan helps you get to your next transaction, better serve your clients and move our industry forward." Accountability and criticism Brown also strongly addressed criticism of NAR, acknowledging the association's shortcomings while challenging critics to provide accurate information. "Accountability starts with being honest about where NAR has fallen short, what must change and whether we are delivering value for you," Brown said. But Brown also took aim at what he characterized as sensationalized coverage of the association. "For some, reporting on NAR’s progress is not a profitable story. Sensationalism sells," Brown said. "We are not interested in fueling miscommunication and half-truths to boost views, profits or egos." Brown maintained that criticism is necessary but said it must be grounded in facts. "We respect our critics," he said. "Honest criticism makes us better and helps hold us accountable." Housing affordability and the future of NAR Brown also highlighted NAR's legislative efforts, including passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act . "It took Realtors to get it across the finish line," Brown said. He also pointed to efforts to modernize credit scoring and help delinquent veteran homeowners avoid foreclosure. As Brown prepares to hand over the presidency to Florida’s Christine Hansen, he acknowledged that the association still has work to do. "NAR is not perfect and our work is not finished," he said. And while he warns that criticism of the association should be based on facts, he insists that members continue to hold NAR accountable. "Keep asking us the hard questions," Brown said. "Keep holding us responsible for clear communication and meaningful results." Related More: MLS National Association of Realtors

items.title: NRMLA asks Congress to restore HUD housing counseling funds
items.description: The National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association ( NRMLA ) is urging Congress to restore funding for the Department of Housing and Urban Development ( HUD )'s housing counseling program, warning that cuts could disrupt the origination of federally insured reverse mortgages. In a Nov. 2 letter to congressional appropriations leaders, NRMLA President Steve Irwin raised concerns about the presidential pocket rescission of appropriated funds for HUD’s housing counseling program, specifically the funding that supports the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) program. NRMLA said independent, third-party counseling is a statutory requirement for every prospective HECM borrower. Under Section 255 of the National Housing Act, borrowers must receive counseling from a HUD-approved agency before a loan can close. A counseling certificate issued by a certified counselor is required for a HECM loan to be legally closed, the trade group said. The association also emphasized that lenders cannot pay for a borrower’s counseling session, direct borrowers to a particular counseling agency or use an agency affiliated with the lender. These restrictions are intended to ensure seniors receive objective information about reverse mortgage costs, obligations and alternatives. Because lenders are prohibited from funding or steering the counseling process, NRMLA said federal appropriations are essential to maintaining the independent counseling infrastructure required for HECM originations. Without the funding, the association warned, mandatory counseling could become less accessible and affordable for seniors, potentially creating obstacles to loan closings and limiting access to the federally insured reverse mortgage program. The HECM program allows eligible older homeowners to access their home equity to support aging in place and improve their financial security. Irwin asked congressional leaders to take action to restore the funds, arguing that the funding is necessary to preserve the program as a housing finance option for seniors. "We respectfully urge you to take the necessary action to restore the appropriated HUD housing counseling funds so that eligible seniors may continue to benefit from the HECM program," he wrote. The association represents more than 300 member companies and more than 2,000 member delegates. Its members originate more than 90% of reverse mortgages , according to the letter. items.title: Strong Economy, Not Inflation, Drives 10-Year Treasury’s Climb
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Weekender | November 5, 2026 By: Amy Wolff Sorter Strong Economy, Not Inflation, Drives 10-Year Treasury’s Climb The 10-year Treasury yield rose nearly 70 basis points from its August low to its early-October peak. According to Cushman & Wakefield’s October Market Matters report, much of that climb reflects a stronger economy, as opposed to lasting inflation fears. That distinction could support commercial real estate returns versus lower rates that might be paired with weaker income growth. What’s Going On “One underappreciated driver of higher Treasury yields is the strength of the economy, itself,” Cushman & Wakefield said. Specifically, stronger consumer spending, coupled with services activity and labor market data, was what led markets to price additional Federal Reserve tightening, with futures assigning “a 40% probability to a (fed funds) rate at least 100 basis points higher by year-end 2027,” Cushman & Wakefield said. The futures match Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s rhetoric. The more robust economy has led to improvement across all CRE sectors: Industrial: Net absorption hit 76.6 million square feet, the highest since the first quarter of 2023, and asking rent growth accelerated to 4%. Multifamily: Vacancy fell to 8.6%, its lowest in three years, and rent growth is the fastest since early 2023. Office: Absorption has been positive for five straight quarters, totaling 15.5 million square feet over the past year. Retail: Vacancy stood at 5.9%, well below its 7.4% historical average. With cap rates unlikely to compress, income growth should drive most total returns going forward, the firm said. Deals Feel the Pressure Still, rate hikes have been putting downward pressure on activity while prompting retrades, as brokers report widening bid-ask spreads. Cushman & Wakefield said accepted retrades have averaged 3% to 5%, “well below requests of roughly 5%-10%.” Some sellers are also pushing transactions out or holding off on new deals. At the same time, owners relying on successive bridge loans to extend hold periods have begun evaluating sales, which Cushman & Wakefield said should materialize in 2027. The firm said that any pricing correction should be milder than during the first rate-hike cycle. Property values are already down approximately 17% as the current basis is 20%-30% below replacement cost. Where Yields Settle Cushman & Wakefield expects the 10-year to settle near 4.5%- 5% as energy shocks wane. This rests on the cost of oil; if it remains above $100 per barrel, impacting core inflation, it ‘would push the entire curve higher,' the report said. In the meantime, near-term yield movements could track shifts in growth sentiment, which would impact CRE. “Underwriting at current rates is the more prudent baseline, and pullbacks like the one in mid-October may offer windows to lock in financing costs,” Cushman & Wakefield said. items.title: Mortgage Rates Tilt Demand Toward Multifamily: Marcus & Millichap
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Weekender | November 5, 2026 By: Amy Wolff Sorter Mortgage Rates Tilt Demand Toward Multifamily: Marcus & Millichap An increase in mortgage rates is cooling home sales, with multifamily the biggest beneficiary, according to John Chang, senior vice president at Marcus & Millichap. In a recent video, Chang said that the 10-year Treasury has risen by more than 100 basis points, and the 30-year mortgage rate is up about 130 bps to the 7.3% range since the start of the Middle East conflict. As a result, the mortgage rate increase has reduced home purchasing power by 8% while “the monthly payment on a $425,000 median priced home back in February would be about the same as the payment on a $390,000 house today,” Chang said. And yes, this has impacted home prices: Pending home sales fell 8.5% from February and 11% from a year earlier Closed existing home sales dropped about 2.2% year over year, as closed sales of new homes dropped by about 5.3% With each home sale generating about $8,700 of retail consumption (including appliances, furniture and renovations), Chang pointed out that a housing market slowdown could moderately impact retail and industrial real estate, while exerting the greatest influence on multifamily. Multifamily stands to feel the greatest impact. Over the past year, the median single-family home price rose 1.2%, but the monthly payment, including principal, interest, taxes and insurance, rose about 8%. Comparatively, apartment rents rose 1.9%. “As a result, the affordability gap between the mortgage payment on a median-priced home using a 10% down payment and the average apartment rent has increased to $1,411, the widest gap on record,” Chang said. “The share of households in the U.S. that can qualify for that mortgage based on the Freddie Mac underwriting guidelines is now just 27%.” This has led to an increase in the median age of the first-time homebuyer. Fifteen years ago, that age was 30; today it’s 40. As such, it’s probably not surprising that multifamily lease renewals are at 57.7%, close to the pandemic-era peak of 58.5% “So, while slackening job creation, slower household formation rates, and a rising number of young adults living with family are all restraining apartment demand. The rising cost of home ownership is at least partially offsetting those trends,” Chang observed. To conclude, as higher interest rates put pressure on home sales, retail and industrial properties could feel some impact. However, it will definitely benefit multifamily investments, especially as construction of all major CRE property types tapers. “But this is a long-term trend that will likely play out over the next couple of years,” Chang said.
